coverage_window.note: UK-focused run covering Sunday 22 November and the night into Monday 23 November. This window was materially busier than the weekend run that preceded it, and the shape of the report changes with it: yesterday's value was in the calendar, today's is in three genuinely new incidents plus a deadline day. THE DOMINANT FACT IS THAT FOUR CISA KEV DEADLINES EXPIRE TODAY - VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890, Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466, Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884 - with the Microsoft Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 following tomorrow, 24 November, the same day the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill returns to the Commons. Rank 1 stays with vCenter and the window settled three things that decide the response: Broadcom revised the advisory to VMSA-2026-0009.1 on 20 November clarifying affected VMware Tools versions, so a change record built from the 19 November original is working from superseded text; the vCenter 7.0 position is now unambiguous, with end of general support since October 2025, no public patch, extended support contract holders directed to Broadcom Support and everyone else facing migration to 8.0 U3m or VCF 9.1; and Broadcom has confirmed that no configuration change mitigates the flaw, leaving blocking TCP 2012 at the firewall as the only control that exists. Rank 2 is the most consequential NEW item for UK government and it is being under-read because Microsoft says customers need do nothing: attackers exploited an Entra Connect Health API flaw, introduced 23 July and detected 9 November, to read tenant ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope and licence tier alongside global administrator and technical contact email addresses. Microsoft fixed it server-side on 19 November. There is no patch to deploy because the vulnerable component was Microsoft's - but the data taken is a verified target list for a sector that runs on Entra ID, and Microsoft's own advice to sign in to the portal directly rather than follow email links is a warning that notification of this incident will itself be impersonated. Rank 3 is tomorrow's governance deadline and the window produced the substance: the Secretary of State has reportedly tabled motions to DISAGREE with both Lords defeats - Lord Camrose's register of foreign powers posing a cyber risk, passed 194-155, and Lord Birt's NIS regime review, passed 202-155 - so the two most widely reported features of the Lords text are the two most likely to disappear. The Bill has also gained two AI clauses, the first of which would let regulators appoint inspectors, enter premises and seize documents after an AI agentic compromise, an incident type the Bill does not define and most UK public bodies cannot currently detect. Rank 4 is Expressway, deadline today, with two new facts: the Russian firm F6 reports attackers used an unnamed AI assistant to exploit it, and Cisco's PSIRT still states it is unaware of exploitation while CISA says it is happening. Rank 5 is new to this feed - ConnectWise ScreenConnect CVE-2026-84869 and the SCKit toolkit, a month-long campaign against MSP technician workstations with 42 servers targeted from 29 IPs and 688,000 malicious run-file requests since 20 October - and it carries the week's most repeated structural trap, because the vulnerable component is the TECHNICIAN CLIENT, not the server the MSP already updated. Rank 6 is the Outlook zero-day whose deadline is tomorrow and whose fix ships through the Office updater rather than Windows Update, so WSUS, Intune and SCCM will all report an estate green while every client stays vulnerable; it now also carries NHS England alert CC-4901 for Ruby, rated Medium but with exploitation assessed as LIKELY and public PoC in existence. Rank 7 is the UK government-facing social engineering window and it opens TODAY: TfL is asking 60-plus photocard holders to revisit its site from 23 November and will ask all 265,000 affected customers to reset passwords and security answers, a publicly announced date and demographic in the aftermath of a breach of their addresses, dates of birth and security answers, alongside HMRC's 1,704 Self Assessment scam reports and a counterfeit GOV.UK refund page. TfL still has not disclosed an initial access vector, a week on. Rank 8 is the Rackspace Spot breach and it is the first item in four runs to come with HARD INDICATORS - 23.224.79.106, the range 23.224.0.0/15, and Kubernetes object prefixes i1, glm- and probe - with the transferable lesson being that the admin console outage prevented customers rotating the very credentials they had been told were compromised. Rank 9 is the UK corporate and supplier cluster at deliberately low confidence, where N0n posted two more UK victims TODAY including a licence-plate recognition analytics firm, Halfords moved from pending to exposed, and the one confirmed incident is Belfast supplier Wellington IT putting roughly 40 credit unions into breach notification six weeks after the event. Rank 10 is the deadline and evidence-quality board, carrying GL.iNet - which updated its breach notice TODAY and whose cloud fix does not remove malware already on devices - plus the Apache Roller fake mitigation, the SAP NetWeaver KEV listing with no published evidence of any kind, a new Tomcat critical with no agreed CVSS score, and the overdue SonicWall SAML-enforced-MFA bypass. THE PATTERN THIS REPORT EXISTS TO NAME: in five separate entries - vCenter 7.0, Expressway, ScreenConnect, Outlook and GL.iNet - the remediation an organisation performed does not cover the component that is vulnerable. And the vendor-versus-authority split appeared THREE times in one day, on vCenter, Expressway and SonicWall, which makes it a systemic property of advisory language rather than a coincidence. Every direct page fetch failed with DNS resolution errors in this run, as in the 21 and 22 November runs - cisa.gov, broadcom.com, digital.nhs.uk, cvebrief.com, thehackernews.com and bills.parliament.uk among them - so this report is built entirely from search-surfaced content and no primary source was read directly.

Ransomware leak-site claims at rank 9 are attacker self-reporting. Bitdefender has documented N0n inflating its victim count by roughly a factor of five, and tracker totals for the group vary by around seventy victims depending on collection method. No UK organisation named in that entry has confirmed an incident.

Several claims in this report rest on a single source and are labelled as such in the relevant entry: the F6 claim that an AI assistant was used to exploit Cisco Expressway; the tabling of the Commons disagreement motions on the CSR Bill; the Wellington IT intrusion dates and method; the claim that an expired certificate was accessed in the Entra Connect Health incident; and the consultancy report that GL.iNet's own detection check misses infections.

Several require log sources that many estates do not forward - vCenter syslog, Expressway syslog, SonicWall syslog, Kubernetes audit logs and request body logging - and several contain placeholder lists that must be populated before they return anything useful.

SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884 is recorded as exploited on the strength of its KEV listing alone. No IOCs, attribution or proof-of-concept have been published by SAP, CISA or Onapsis, and one source states no public exploitation evidence exists.

Apache Tomcat CVE-2026-133325 carries an unresolved CVSS scoring conflict: one source cites 9.8, others state no score is published or describe it as unscored. The entry records the disagreement rather than choosing a figure.

The exploitation predicted at rank 7, a phishing campaign exploiting the TfL breach and its announced 23 November return date, has not been observed. It is this feed's inference from the published calendar and data categories, and the entry's exploitation status is set to attempts-reported-unconfirmed accordingly.

vulnerabilities.title: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890: THE KEV DEADLINE IS TODAY, and the Window Confirms the Three Things That Decide Your Response - Broadcom Revised the Advisory to VMSA-2026-0009.1, There Is Still No Public 7.0 Patch, and Blocking TCP 2012 Is the Only Mitigation That Exists
affected_products: VMware vCenter Server 9.1.x - fixed in 9.1.1.0200
VMware vCenter Server 9.0.x - fixed in 9.0.2.0200
VMware vCenter Server 8.0.x - fixed in 8.0 U3m
VMware vCenter Server 7.0.x - END OF GENERAL SUPPORT SINCE OCTOBER 2025, no public patch, extended support contract holders directed to Broadcom Support
VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - requires vCenter 8.0 U3m plus SDDC Manager 5.2.5
Vulnerable component: vCenter Directory Service (vmdird), TCP 2012
NOT eligible for vCenter Quick Patch - this is a full update
vulnerabilities.summary:
This holds rank 1 for a third day, and today the reason is arithmetic rather than analysis: the CISA KEV remediation deadline for CVE-2026-123890 is TODAY, Monday 23 November. If your organisation is a UK public body applying KEV as a de facto standard - and most now do, because NHS England Digital, the NCSC and departmental assurance teams all lean on it - then the window to patch without writing a risk acceptance closes at the end of today.

What the flaw is. CVE-2026-123890 is a CVSS 9.8 authentication bypass in the vCenter Directory Service, the identity component that backs vSphere SSO. A network-positioned attacker who can reach the service obtains full administrator access to vCenter without any password. From vCenter, the attacker inherits the hypervisor estate: every virtual machine, every datastore, every snapshot, and the ability to mint and present credentials to everything that trusts vSphere SSO.

Three things the 22-23 November window settled, each of which changes what you do today.

FIRST, the advisory has been revised. Broadcom published VMSA-2026-0009 on 19 November and revised it to VMSA-2026-0009.1 on 20 November, clarifying the affected VMware Tools versions. If your change record, your CAB paper or your patch bundle was assembled from the original advisory on 19 or 20 November, it is built on superseded text. Re-read the .1 revision before you close the ticket, because the Tools clarification changes which guest-side work is in scope.

SECOND, the vCenter 7.0 position is now unambiguous, and it is worse than 'no patch yet'. vCenter 7.0 reached end of general support in October 2025. There is no public fix and there will not be one. Broadcom directs customers holding extended support contracts to contact Broadcom Support; customers without such a contract have no patch route at all and their only path is migration to vCenter 8.0 U3m or VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1. This feed has flagged the 7.0 gap for three consecutive days, first as a single-source claim, then as corroborated by the absence of a 7.0 build in the fixed list, and now as a stated support position. For every UK estate still on the 7.0 branch - and in local government, NHS trusts and universities running long hardware refresh cycles there are many - today is not a patching decision. It is a decision with three options and a named owner: buy extended support and raise a case with Broadcom today, accelerate a migration that was probably already late, or isolate the vCenter instance from everything that does not strictly need to reach it. Choosing none of those is also a decision, and it is the one that will be read back to you in an inquiry.

THIRD, there is exactly one mitigation and it is a firewall rule. Broadcom has confirmed that no configuration change and no feature toggle mitigates this flaw. The only partial risk reduction available is blocking TCP port 2012 at the firewall and permitting it only from authorised vCenter peer addresses. That is the control to put in place within the hour if you cannot patch today, and it is also the control to put in place permanently afterwards, because port 2012 is a replication and directory port that has no business being reachable from a user VLAN, a VPN pool or the internet.

The exploitation picture, and why patching is not the end of it. Google's Mandiant attributes zero-day exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-linked espionage group, with activity beginning in early September 2026 - approximately ten weeks before the 19 November fix. Mandiant's CTO has stated publicly that the firm investigated multiple intrusions through this flaw, which remains the strongest available evidence that real compromise occurred rather than scanning. Ten weeks of pre-patch access against an identity component means that applying the update today closes the entry route and evicts nobody. The hunting work is the deliverable, not the patch.

The vendor-versus-authority split persists and it is a governance finding in its own right. Reporting in this window continues to state that Broadcom's advisory and FAQ do not confirm in-the-wild exploitation, while CISA's KEV entry, NHS England Digital's alert and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security all do. Any triage process that takes vendor severity text as its exploitation signal scored this as a routine critical. That is the process to fix after today's patching is done.

Confidence. High on the CVE, the 9.8 score, the Directory Service component, the 19 November fix date, the VMSA-2026-0009.1 revision on 20 November, the fixed build numbers, the 7.0 end-of-general-support position, the absence of any configuration mitigation, the TCP 2012 firewall recommendation, the KEV listing dated 20 November and the 23 November deadline. High on ARMORY CASTLE attribution and September start, which Mandiant has published. Medium on the precise content of the Tools clarification in the .1 revision, which this feed could not read directly - every attempt to fetch broadcom.com, cisa.gov and digital.nhs.uk failed on DNS resolution in this run, as in the two previous runs.
recommended_actions: PATCH TODAY. The KEV deadline is 23 November. Fixed builds are vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x needs vCenter 8.0 U3m with SDDC Manager 5.2.5. This is not eligible for vCenter Quick Patch, so plan for a full update and a reboot window.

Re-read VMSA-2026-0009.1 before closing the change. Broadcom revised the advisory on 20 November to clarify affected VMware Tools versions. A change record built from the 19 November original is working from superseded text and may have the guest-side scope wrong.

Block TCP 2012 at the firewall now, permitting it only from authorised vCenter peer addresses. Broadcom has confirmed there is no configuration or feature-toggle mitigation, so this is the only compensating control that exists. It needs no maintenance window and should remain in place permanently after patching.

If you are on vCenter 7.0, make the decision today and name the owner. There is no public patch and 7.0 left general support in October 2025. Option one: if you hold an extended support contract, raise a case with Broadcom Support today. Option two: accelerate migration to 8.0 U3m or VCF 9.1. Option three: isolate the instance. Record which one you chose and who signed it.

Hunt as though you were compromised, because exploitation ran from early September to the 19 November fix. Enumerate every administrator account in vsphere.local against your change records and look for accounts created, re-enabled or re-scoped between 1 September and the date you patched.

Check for access to, or copies of, /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb. That file is the directory database. Its theft is the difference between an intrusion you can remediate by patching and one you cannot.

Decide this week whether to rotate the SAML STS signing certificate and key material. An attacker holding that material can mint valid assertions for every service that trusts your vSphere SSO, and no password reset revokes it. This is disruptive, which is why it needs a decision rather than a default.

Review vCenter and ESXi for unexpected virtual machine clones, snapshot exports, datastore browse activity and new local accounts over the September-to-November period. Hypervisor-level data theft leaves traces in vCenter task and event logs rather than in guest EDR.

Confirm your vCenter appliances forward syslog to Sentinel or an equivalent. Several of the hunting queries in this entry are useless without it, and many UK estates monitor the guests while leaving the control plane unmonitored.

Raise the vendor-text-versus-authority gap as a process finding. Broadcom's advisory reportedly still does not state exploitation while CISA, NHS England Digital and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security all do. If your triage reads vendor severity as the exploitation signal, it will under-rank the next one of these too.

kql.name: Connections to vCenter Directory Service TCP 2012 from outside the authorised peer set
kql.description: Primary network detection and the direct counterpart to Broadcom's only stated mitigation. Populate vcenterPeers with your authorised vCenter peer addresses; anything else reaching 2012 is either a misconfiguration or an exploitation attempt. External sources should be treated as incidents.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let vcenterPeers = dynamic([]);  // populate with authorised vCenter peer IPs
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort == 2012
| extend PeerAuthorised = iff(array_length(vcenterPeers) > 0 and SourceIP in (vcenterPeers), true, false)
| where PeerAuthorised == false
| extend SourceIsExternal = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Attempts = count(), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 5)
    by SourceIP, SourceIsExternal
| order by SourceIsExternal desc, Attempts desc

kql.name: vCenter Directory Service authentication anomalies across the exploitation window
kql.description: Surfaces vmdird and SSO authentication events on vCenter appliances. Exploitation is an authentication bypass, so look for administrative sessions that have no matching credential presentation. Requires vCenter syslog forwarding.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
let exploitStart = datetime(2026-09-01);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vc-", "vcenter-appliance")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("vmdird", "vmdir", "sts", "websso", "vsphere.local", "authentication", "LDAP bind", "SAML")
| extend InExploitWindow = TimeGenerated >= exploitStart
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, InExploitWindow, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Access to or copying of the vmdir directory database file
kql.description: /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb is the directory database. Theft of this file converts a patchable intrusion into an identity compromise. Any read, copy, archive or transfer reference is a high-priority lead.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vc-")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("data.mdb", "vmware-vmdir", "/storage/db", "vmdir.ldif", "vdcbackup", "vdcrepadmin")
    or (SyslogMessage has_any ("tar", "gzip", "scp", "curl", "wget", "cp ") and SyslogMessage has "storage")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: New, re-enabled or re-scoped vsphere.local SSO administrator accounts since 1 September
kql.description: Exploitation grants administrator access without a password, and persistence is commonly an account. Compare every hit against change records for the September-to-patch window.
kql.query:
let exploitStart = datetime(2026-09-01);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated >= exploitStart
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vc-")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("vsphere.local", "SSO", "Administrators", "SystemConfiguration.Administrators", "TrustedAdmins")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("create", "created", "add", "added", "enable", "enabled", "role", "grant", "permission", "password reset")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Unexpected VM clone, snapshot export and datastore browse activity on the hypervisor control plane
kql.description: Hypervisor-level data theft does not touch guest EDR. This surfaces the vCenter task and event vocabulary associated with cloning, exporting and datastore file access so it can be reconciled against change records.
kql.query:
let exploitStart = datetime(2026-09-01);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated >= exploitStart
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vc-", "esxi", "esx-")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("CloneVM_Task", "ExportVm", "CreateSnapshot_Task", "DatastoreBrowser", "SearchDatastore", "ovftool", "vmdk", "HttpNfcLease")
| summarize Events = count(), Samples = make_set(SyslogMessage, 5) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Downstream federated authentication anomalies consistent with forged vSphere SSO assertions
kql.description: If SAML STS signing material was taken, an attacker can mint valid assertions. This looks for federated sign-ins with impossible geography or absent MFA interaction that could indicate assertion replay rather than real authentication. Tune to your federation topology.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication" or isempty(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend Method = tostring(parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)[0].authenticationMethod)
| where Method has_any ("Federated", "Previously satisfied", "") or isempty(Method)
| summarize Signins = count(), Countries = make_set(Location, 10), IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
    by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where IPs > 3 or array_length(Countries) > 2
| order by IPs desc

kql.name: Endpoint-side view of hosts reaching vCenter management ports
kql.description: Catches the client end of the same activity, which is useful where the firewall does not log internal east-west traffic. A workstation or non-admin server reaching 2012 is anomalous by definition.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemotePort in (2012, 443, 902, 9443)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa") or RemoteIP != ""
| where RemotePort == 2012
| summarize Connections = count(), Targets = make_set(RemoteIP, 10), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.title: NEW: Microsoft Confirms Attackers Exploited an Entra Connect Health API Flaw to Read Tenant Administrator Email Addresses and Configuration Metadata - Introduced 23 July, Detected 9 November, Fixed 19 November, and Microsoft Says Customers Need Do Nothing, Which Is Exactly Why UK Public Sector Admins Should Act
affected_products: Microsoft Entra Connect Health - cloud service API
Microsoft Entra ID tenants that had Entra Connect Health agents reporting in
Exposed record fields reported: tenant ID, tenant display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope, licence tier
Exposed contact data reported: global administrator and technical contact email addresses
Fix applied server-side by Microsoft on 19 November 2026 - no customer-installable update exists
vulnerabilities.summary:
This is the most consequential genuinely new item in the window for UK government, and it is being widely under-read because Microsoft's own notice says customers need take no remediation action. That statement is true about software updates and false about risk.

What happened. Microsoft has confirmed that an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in the Entra Connect Health API and read tenant data. The timeline it has given is unusually precise and unusually uncomfortable: the flaw was introduced on 23 July 2026, detected on 9 November 2026, and fixed on Microsoft's own servers on 19 November 2026, with affected organisations notified from that date and the investigation concluding around 20 November. That is a one-hundred-and-nine-day exposure window in a first-party identity telemetry service, with ten days between detection and fix.

What was taken. Access was read-only. The records reported as exposed are tenant ID, tenant display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope and licence tier, together with the email addresses of global administrators and technical contacts. Microsoft states it found no unauthorised configuration changes, and reporting is consistent that no mailbox contents, no message bodies, no passwords and no authentication tokens were exposed.

Why this matters disproportionately to UK government. Entra ID is the identity substrate of UK central government, the NHS, local authorities and the university sector. Entra Connect Health is the service that reports on the health of hybrid identity synchronisation - which means the tenants most likely to appear in this dataset are precisely the large, hybrid, on-premises-plus-cloud estates that characterise the UK public sector. The data taken is not sensitive in the ordinary sense. It is a target list. An attacker now holding a verified mapping of tenant display name to initial domain to named global administrator email address to licence tier has everything needed to construct a phishing or help-desk social engineering approach that is accurate in every checkable detail: the right organisation name, the right onmicrosoft.com domain, the right administrator, the right product entitlements. Accuracy is what defeats user scepticism, and this dataset supplies it.

The second-order risk, and the reason Microsoft's 'no action required' framing is dangerous. Microsoft advises administrators to sign in directly to the Azure portal and check the Security Advisory in Azure Service Health rather than following links in email. Read that advice carefully: Microsoft is warning that notification of this incident will itself be impersonated. A global administrator who receives an email that correctly names their tenant, correctly names their initial domain, correctly addresses them by name and asks them to review a Microsoft security advisory is being handed a lure with no detectable inaccuracy. In a UK public body where the global administrator population often includes contractors and shared service staff, that is a credible route to an administrative credential.

What Microsoft has not said. It has not disclosed how many tenants were affected, who the attacker was, or when the attack activity began within the 23 July to 9 November window. It has not published indicators. There is no CVE. One secondary source claims an expired certificate was also accessed; this feed treats that as unverified because it appears in a single aggregator.

The honest assessment. There is no patch to deploy and no log to check on your own infrastructure, because the vulnerable component was Microsoft's. What there is, is a window in which your named administrators are known to an attacker who also knows your tenant's identifying details. The correct response is not technical remediation. It is to confirm whether you were notified, to tell your administrator population directly and through a channel that is not email, to tighten the help-desk verification path that administrative credential resets run through, and to hunt for consent grants and sign-in anomalies on privileged accounts across the exposure window. That work is cheap and it is the only work available.

Confidence. High on the incident, the read-only nature of the access, the 23 July introduction, 9 November detection and 19 November server-side fix, the exposed field list, the absence of mailbox content and token exposure, Microsoft's statement that no configuration changes were made, and Microsoft's advice to verify through Azure Service Health rather than email links. Medium on the end-of-investigation date of 20 November. Low on the claimed expired certificate access, which is single-source. Unknown: tenant count, attacker identity, start of malicious activity.
recommended_actions: Check Azure Service Health for the Security Advisory, signing in to the portal directly rather than following any link in an email. If your tenant was affected, Microsoft has posted it there. This is also the verification step for any email you receive claiming to be about this incident.

Tell your global administrators and technical contacts directly, through Teams, phone or in person rather than email, that their addresses are in a dataset an attacker holds alongside your tenant's identifying details. Specifically warn them that a convincing lure will name the organisation, the initial domain and them personally, and will be accurate in every detail they would normally check.

Harden the help-desk verification path for administrative password and MFA resets this week. The realistic attack here is a phone call or ticket from someone who can quote the tenant display name, initial domain and licence tier correctly. If your verification relies on knowledge an attacker now has, change it to something they do not: a callback to an HR-held number, or in-person verification.

Hunt privileged account sign-ins and consent grants across 23 July to 19 November 2026. There is no evidence of credential compromise, but the exposure window is the only period in which to look, and consent grants to newly registered applications are the cheapest high-value check available.

Audit and reduce the global administrator population. The size of that population is now directly proportional to this incident's attack surface, and in many UK public bodies it includes contractors, suppliers and shared service staff who should hold scoped roles instead.

Require phishing-resistant MFA for every account holding a privileged Entra role, if you have not already. The data taken enables targeting, not authentication; phishing-resistant factors are what make accurate targeting fail anyway.

Record the exposure in your risk register and notify your SIRO or equivalent. For UK public bodies this is a supplier-side confidentiality incident affecting administrative contact data. Microsoft stating that no customer action is required does not mean no governance record is required.

Review whether Entra Connect Health agents are deployed more widely than they need to be, and whether the technical contact addresses registered in your tenant are role mailboxes rather than named individuals. Role mailboxes are materially harder to social-engineer against.
Do not wait for a CVE or IOCs. None have been published, none are likely, and the useful actions in this entry do not depend on them.

kql.name: OAuth consent grants and application registrations across the Entra Connect Health exposure window
kql.description: The highest-value cheap check. If targeting of administrators succeeded, a consent grant or new application registration is the most common quiet outcome. Scoped to 23 July to 19 November 2026.
kql.query:
let windowStart = datetime(2026-07-23);
let windowEnd = datetime(2026-11-19);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (windowStart .. windowEnd)
| where OperationName has_any ("Consent to application", "Add service principal", "Add app role assignment", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant", "Update application")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, Target, Result, CorrelationId
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Privileged Entra role assignments and administrative changes during the exposure window
kql.description: Microsoft states it found no unauthorised configuration changes in its own service. This checks your tenant independently for role escalation across the same period, which is the assurance your auditors will ask for.
kql.query:
let windowStart = datetime(2026-07-23);
let windowEnd = datetime(2026-11-19);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (windowStart .. windowEnd)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add member to role", "Add eligible member to role", "Update role", "Add owner to application", "Reset user password", "Update StsRefreshTokenValidFrom Timestamp", "Disable Strong Authentication")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend TargetUser = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| extend RoleName = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[1].newValue)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, TargetUser, RoleName, Result
| order by TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Sign-ins by global administrators and technical contacts from new countries or new autonomous systems
kql.description: The exposed dataset is a target list of named administrators. This looks for first-seen geography and first-seen network for exactly that population. Populate the adminUpns list from your tenant's privileged role holders and registered technical contacts.
kql.query:
let lookback = 150d;
let adminUpns = dynamic([]);  // populate with global admin and technical contact UPNs
let baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(60d))
    | where array_length(adminUpns) == 0 or UserPrincipalName in~ (adminUpns)
    | summarize KnownCountries = make_set(Location, 50), KnownAsns = make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber, 50) by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where array_length(adminUpns) == 0 or UserPrincipalName in~ (adminUpns)
| join kind=leftouter baseline on UserPrincipalName
| where Location !in (KnownCountries) or AutonomousSystemNumber !in (KnownAsns)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, Location, AutonomousSystemNumber, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Service principal sign-ins associated with Entra Connect Health and hybrid identity tooling
kql.description: Checks the non-interactive side. Entra Connect Health agents authenticate as service principals; anomalous source addresses or result codes for that population are worth reconciling even though the exploited component was Microsoft's.
kql.query:
let lookback = 150d;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ServicePrincipalName has_any ("Connect Health", "AzureADConnect", "Entra Connect", "Health", "Sync")
    or AppId in ("4c9d2ba0-ad2f-4bc1-a9fd-c38fbfc97d8c")
| summarize Signins = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), 10), Results = make_set(ResultType, 10)
    by ServicePrincipalName, AppId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Inbound mail to privileged administrators referencing Microsoft security advisories or tenant identifiers
kql.description: Directly addresses the real risk. An attacker holding tenant display name, initial domain and named administrator addresses will send mail that is accurate in every checkable detail. Replace the placeholders with your own tenant strings.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
let adminAddresses = dynamic([]);  // populate with global admin and technical contact addresses
let tenantStrings = dynamic(["onmicrosoft.com"]);  // add your tenant display name and initial domain
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where array_length(adminAddresses) == 0 or RecipientEmailAddress in~ (adminAddresses)
| where Subject has_any ("security advisory", "Service Health", "Entra", "Azure AD", "tenant", "administrator action required", "Connect Health")
    or Subject has_any (tenantStrings)
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, ThreatTypes, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Help-desk-pattern credential resets and MFA changes on privileged accounts
kql.description: The realistic exploitation path is social engineering of the help desk using accurate tenant detail. This surfaces reset and MFA-change activity on privileged accounts so each one can be matched to a verified ticket.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType has_any ("Account Password Changed", "Account Password Reset", "User Account Modified", "Group Membership changed", "Account Enabled")
| extend TargetAccount = tostring(TargetAccountUpn)
| summarize Events = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10), Actors = make_set(AccountUpn, 10) by TargetAccount, bin(Timestamp, 1d)
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: TOMORROW: The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill Returns to the Commons on Tuesday 24 November, and the Government Has Tabled Motions to DISAGREE With Both Lords Defeats - Plus Two New AI Clauses Including Inspection and Seizure Powers After an AI-Agent Compromise
affected_products: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill 2024-26, UK Parliament Bill 4035
In scope: operators of essential services and relevant digital service providers under the NIS Regulations 2018 successor regime
Newly in scope under Lords amendments: third-party vendors subject to Secretary of State direction on national security grounds
Newly in scope: deployers of AI agents, where the Secretary of State makes regulations following an AI-agent compromise
Affected UK bodies: central government departments, NHS organisations, local authorities, utilities, transport operators, digital infrastructure and managed service providers
vulnerabilities.summary:
The governance deadline in this report is tomorrow, and the window has produced the detail that makes it worth acting on rather than merely noting.

The mechanics. The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill has completed its Lords stages and returns to the Commons on Tuesday 24 November 2026 for consideration of Lords amendments. The House of Commons Library confirms the date and the Parliament stages page for Bill 4035 lists it. Yesterday's run recorded this date as newly confirmed; today it is tomorrow, and the substance of what MPs will vote on is now visible.

The new and material fact: the Government is fighting both defeats. Reporting in this window states that the Secretary of State, Lisa Nandy, has tabled motions 'That this House disagrees with the Lords' on both of the Opposition amendments that defeated the Government in the Lords. Those two amendments are identified as Lord Camrose's requirement for a register of foreign powers posing a risk to UK cyber security, and Lord Birt's requirement for a review of the UK's NIS regime. They passed the Lords by 194 to 155 and 202 to 155 respectively. MPs will decide the disagreement motions first. The practical consequence for anyone planning compliance work is that the two most widely reported features of the Lords text - the hostile state actor register and the whole-regime review - are the two features most likely to disappear tomorrow. Do not build either into a gap analysis this week.

The AI clauses, which are the genuinely novel content. Since the September text the Bill has gained two AI provisions. The first, introduced at Lords third reading, would let ministers make regulations allowing regulators to appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, and seize and retain documents following an AI agentic compromise - that is, after an incident in which control of an AI agent was lost. Pinsent Masons' Stuart Davey has characterised the clause as 'quite novel', which is lawyerly for unprecedented. Critically, public reporting does not show the Bill text defining either 'AI agent' or 'loss of control'; those definitions would be set by the Secretary of State in secondary legislation, subject to consultation and parliamentary approval. The second provision is an annual review covering sectors including cloud services and frontier AI, and considering whether the AI Security Institute should acquire audit, inspection or restriction powers over frontier AI systems. Lord Clement-Jones additionally pressed for last-resort powers to shut down data centres or large-scale AI systems in an emergency; this feed could not confirm whether those were adopted.

Why a UK public body should care about the AI clauses specifically. Every UK department, NHS organisation and large local authority is currently deploying AI agents with privileged access to internal systems - service desk automation, document triage, coding assistants with repository access. If the Bill passes with the agentic compromise clause, the event that triggers inspection and document seizure powers is an incident type that most of those organisations currently have no definition of, no detection for, no logging of and no incident response playbook for. The gap is not legal. It is operational: if a regulator can enter your premises and seize documents following an AI agent compromise, you need to be able to tell when one has happened, which requires that agent actions be logged in an attributable, retained, reviewable form. Almost nobody is doing that today.

The other Lords changes, from the Commons Library list. Government-added clauses give the Secretary of State powers over third-party vendors on national security grounds. The Library also records a narrowed incident reporting definition and limits on information sharing with overseas jurisdictions. Third-party trackers additionally report that mandatory near-miss reporting was dropped. One guide states that MPs will consider 112 Lords amendments tomorrow; other sources discuss only a handful, so the total is unverified.

The practical instruction, repeated from yesterday because it is more urgent today. If your CSRB gap analysis predates 2 November 2026 it is written against a superseded text. That is worse than having no gap analysis, because it creates documented confidence in conclusions that have changed. Hold the analysis until Wednesday, then rebuild it against what actually survives tomorrow's votes.

Confidence. High on the 24 November date, the completion of Lords stages, the government clauses on third-party vendors, the two Opposition amendments and their Lords division results, the existence of the agentic compromise clause and the frontier AI review, and the fact that the Bill text does not define 'AI agent' or 'loss of control'. Medium on the tabling of the disagreement motions, which comes from secondary commentary rather than the Order Paper, and on the narrowed incident definition and dropped near-miss reporting. Low on the 112-amendment figure and on the fate of the data centre shutdown powers. Parliament's own pages could not be read directly in this run - all page fetches failed on DNS resolution.
recommended_actions: Watch tomorrow's votes before you change anything. The two amendments most widely reported as the Lords' contribution - the register of foreign powers posing a cyber risk, and the NIS regime review - are the two the Government has tabled motions to disagree with. They may not survive the day.

Hold any CSRB gap analysis until Wednesday 25 November. If yours predates 2 November 2026 it is written against superseded text, and a documented analysis with changed conclusions is worse than none. Rebuild it against the post-ping-pong text.

Start the AI agent logging work now, because it does not depend on the vote. Identify every AI agent deployed in your organisation that holds privileged access to internal systems, and establish whether its actions are logged in an attributable, retained and reviewable form. If a regulator can seize documents after an AI-agent compromise, you need to be able to detect one.

Write a working definition of 'AI agent compromise' and 'loss of control' for your own incident taxonomy, and do not wait for the statutory one. The Bill leaves both to secondary legislation, which means there will be a period in which the duty exists and the definition does not. An internal definition is better than a vacuum.

Add AI-agent incident scenarios to your incident response plan and exercise one. Most UK public bodies have no playbook for an agent that took unintended privileged action, and the inspection and seizure powers in the clause attach to exactly that event.

Map your third-party vendor dependencies against the new Secretary of State direction powers on national security grounds. If a direction could require you to remove or replace a vendor, know now which vendors are plausible candidates and what the replacement path looks like.

Re-check your incident reporting thresholds against the narrowed incident definition and the reported removal of mandatory near-miss reporting. A reporting process built for the September text may now over-report, which is less dangerous than under-reporting but still a cost.

Review restrictions on sharing incident information with overseas jurisdictions against your existing arrangements, particularly if you use a non-UK managed security provider, a non-UK SIEM tenancy or a group parent outside the UK. This is the clause most likely to conflict with existing supplier contracts.

Assign a named owner for CSRB readiness with authority across IT, legal, procurement and risk. The Bill's duties cut across all four, and the organisations that will struggle are those where cyber compliance sits entirely inside IT.

kql.name: Inventory of AI agent and automation service principals holding privileged access
kql.description: Foundation work for the agentic compromise clause. You cannot detect an AI agent compromise without knowing which non-human identities exist and what they can reach. This enumerates service principals and app registrations whose naming suggests AI or agentic automation.
kql.query:
let lookback = 180d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add service principal", "Add app role assignment", "Consent to application", "Add delegated permission grant")
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| where AppName has_any ("agent", "copilot", "gpt", "llm", "assistant", "bot", "automation", "openai", "anthropic", "claude", "gemini", "bedrock", "autogen", "langchain")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| summarize Grants = count(), Operations = make_set(OperationName, 10), Actors = make_set(Actor, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by AppName
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: Non-human identity activity volume and geography baseline for AI agents
kql.description: Establishes the baseline you will need in order to recognise a loss-of-control event. An AI agent whose request volume, source network or target application set changes sharply is the operational signature of the incident type the Bill creates powers over.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ServicePrincipalName has_any ("agent", "copilot", "gpt", "llm", "assistant", "bot", "automation")
| summarize Signins = count(), Apps = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion), 10)
    by ServicePrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by ServicePrincipalName asc, TimeGenerated asc

kql.name: Privilege expansion of automation and agent identities over time
kql.description: Loss of control is often preceded by scope creep that nobody reviewed. This surfaces permission and role additions to agent-shaped identities so each can be reconciled against an approval.
kql.query:
let lookback = 180d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add app role assignment to service principal", "Add delegated permission grant", "Add member to role", "Update application - Certificates and secrets management")
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| where Target has_any ("agent", "copilot", "gpt", "llm", "assistant", "bot", "automation")
| extend NewValue = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[0].newValue)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Target, NewValue, Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Bulk data access by automation identities - the detectable shape of an agentic compromise
kql.description: The operational signature most likely to matter: an agent reading far more than its function requires. Thresholds are deliberately crude and must be tuned to your own agents' legitimate volumes before use.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where isnotempty(AccountDisplayName)
| where AccountDisplayName has_any ("agent", "copilot", "gpt", "llm", "assistant", "bot", "automation", "svc-", "service")
| where ActionType has_any ("FileDownloaded", "FileAccessed", "FileSyncDownloadedFull", "SearchQueryPerformed", "MailItemsAccessed", "Export")
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 10)
    by AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Actions > 500 or DistinctObjects > 200
| order by Actions desc

kql.name: Outbound traffic from internal systems to external AI inference endpoints
kql.description: Supports the vendor direction and overseas information sharing clauses as well as agent inventory. Identifies which internal systems send data to which external model providers, which is the dependency map those clauses will require.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
let aiDomains = dynamic(["openai.com", "api.openai.com", "anthropic.com", "api.anthropic.com", "generativelanguage.googleapis.com", "bedrock", "cohere.ai", "mistral.ai", "huggingface.co", "azure-api.net"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationHostName has_any (aiDomains) or RequestURL has_any (aiDomains)
| summarize Sessions = count(), BytesOut = sum(SentBytes), Destinations = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20), Users = make_set(SourceUserName, 20)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by BytesOut desc

vulnerabilities.title: Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466: KEV DEADLINE TODAY, and the Window Adds Two Things That Change the Picture - Attackers Reportedly Used an AI Assistant to Exploit It, and Cisco's PSIRT Still Says It Is Unaware of Exploitation While CISA Says It Is Happening
affected_products: Cisco Expressway-C - clustered deployments only
Cisco Expressway-E - clustered deployments only
Cisco TelePresence Video Communication Server (VCS) Expressway - same advisory family (cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t)
Vulnerable component: cluster database service, Erlang-based, TCP 4371-4372
Fixed release: X15.5.20
Non-clustered Expressway deployments reported as not affected
Original Cisco disclosure: 21 October 2026
vulnerabilities.summary:
Second of today's four expiring KEV deadlines, and the one with the most interesting new detail.

The flaw, restated because the scope matters. CVE-2026-76466 is a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability in the cluster database service of clustered Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E. Reporting in this window characterises it as hard-coded credentials combined with a failure to fully validate client certificates, enabling an unauthenticated attacker to execute operating system commands as root. The service is Erlang-based and listens on TCP 4372, with 4371 named alongside it in mitigation guidance. The maintenance identity and its Erlang cookie are compiled into the software and identical on every installation, so there is nothing to rotate and no password policy that helps. The fix is X15.5.20 and Cisco states explicitly that no workaround eliminates the vulnerability. Only clustered deployments are affected - worth confirming before you schedule emergency downtime on a clinical or public-facing video service.

NEW, AND THE REASON THIS ENTRY IS WORTH RE-READING: an AI assistant was reportedly used in the exploitation. The Russian security firm F6 states it observed attackers using an unnamed AI assistant to exploit this flaw and obtain root command execution on internet-exposed devices, having initially compromised two internet-facing Cisco Expressway devices. Set aside the attribution question for a moment and consider what that claim means operationally. It is consistent with the chain this feed reported yesterday - two edge nodes breached, pivot to two internal cluster members, then custom Python scripts scanning SMB, SQL Server and WinRM and harvesting credentials from internal GitLab repositories. An AI-assisted operator produces exactly that profile: fast exploitation of a freshly published flaw, followed by competent but generic post-exploitation tooling written on the fly. It also matters for the UK specifically, because the NCSC's annual review on 3 November warned that AI-enabled attack capability is arriving faster than defensive capability, and this is the first item in this feed's coverage where a named vendor claims to have watched it happen against a specific CVE. Treat the specific claim as medium confidence - F6 is a single source, the AI assistant is unnamed, and 'used an AI assistant' is an inherently difficult thing to evidence from network telemetry.

NEW, AND A PROBLEM FOR YOUR TRIAGE PROCESS: Cisco and CISA disagree in public. Cisco's PSIRT states it is not aware of active exploitation in the wild or of public proof-of-concept code. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 20 November on the basis of evidence of active exploitation, with a federal deadline of today. This is the second entry in today's report - after vCenter at rank 1 - where the vendor's advisory text and the national authority's exploitation determination point in opposite directions. If your vulnerability management process derives urgency from vendor language, it scored both of today's most urgent items as routine. That is now a demonstrated, repeated failure mode rather than a theoretical one, and it is worth a paragraph in your next assurance report.

The disclosure timeline is longer than most people think. Cisco first disclosed this on 21 October 2026. It has therefore been public for over a month, and today's KEV deadline is not the start of the clock but the end of it. If your organisation has clustered Expressway and has not patched, the honest framing for your risk acceptance is that the fix has been available for five weeks.

Why this lands hard on UK government. Expressway and VCS are the standard Cisco edge for Mobile and Remote Access and business-to-business video, deployed across NHS trusts, local authorities, central government departments and universities, frequently with Expressway-E deliberately internet-facing because that is its function. The architecture that makes Expressway useful is the architecture the vulnerability exploits.

The highest-value action if you cannot patch today remains a firewall rule: restrict TCP 4371-4372 at the boundary to trusted cluster nodes only. Because the credential is universal and unchangeable, port reachability is effectively the entire exposure, and the rule requires no maintenance window. But do not stop at the appliance. The reported objective was credentials in internal GitLab repositories. Patch Expressway and leave your repositories full of service account passwords and you have closed the door and left the keys outside.

Confidence. High on the CVE, the 9.8 score, hard-coded credentials, the Erlang cluster database service, TCP 4371-4372, root-level impact, X15.5.20 as the fix, the absence of a workaround, clustered-only scope, the 21 October Cisco disclosure, the 20 November KEV addition, the 23 November deadline, and the Cisco-versus-CISA exploitation disagreement. Medium on the AI assistant claim, which rests on F6 alone, and on the intrusion chain detail including GitLab credential theft, which comes from secondary reporting with no named victim or actor. One source previously raised a CVE-to-advisory mapping concern; this feed still could not verify it against cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t directly because all page fetches failed on DNS resolution.
recommended_actions: Restrict TCP 4371-4372 at the boundary to trusted cluster nodes only, right now, if you have not already. The Erlang cookie is compiled in and identical on every install, so reachability is the entire exposure. No maintenance window required, and this is the single highest-value action in the entry.

Upgrade clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E to X15.5.20. The KEV deadline is today and the fix has been available since Cisco's 21 October disclosure. There is no workaround, so the alternatives are the firewall rule plus a written risk acceptance.

Confirm whether your deployment is actually clustered before scheduling emergency downtime. Non-clustered deployments are reported as unaffected, and unnecessary emergency change on a clinical video service carries real patient-facing risk.

Audit internal GitLab and every other internal source control system for credentials, and rotate what you find. The reported objective of the intrusion chain was pulling credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Patching the appliance does not remove secrets already committed to repositories.
Rotate every credential a compromised Expressway node could have reached, prioritising service accounts, API keys and database connection strings over user passwords.

Treat all cluster peers as compromised if any single node was reachable and unpatched. The reported chain moved from internet-facing nodes to internal cluster members because they trust each other by design and share the same compiled-in cookie.

Hunt the post-exploitation behaviour rather than just the version string: Python processes on or originating from Expressway nodes, SMB share enumeration, and SQL Server and WinRM probing from the video edge segment. These distinguish exploited from merely vulnerable.

Raise the Cisco-versus-CISA disagreement as a process finding alongside the identical vCenter finding at rank 1. Two of today's four expiring deadlines involve a vendor advisory that does not assert exploitation and a national authority that does. If your triage keys on vendor language, fix that this quarter.

Review why Expressway-E was reachable on 4372 from outside at all. The service exists for cluster replication, not for clients. If your boundary policy permitted it, scan your perimeter from outside and find out what else it permitted.

Verify the CVE-to-advisory mapping against cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t before finalising your change record. One source previously reported that the advisory text it retrieved did not name CVE-2026-76466, and this feed has still not been able to confirm either way.

kql.name: Inbound connections to Expressway cluster database ports TCP 4371-4372
kql.description: Primary detection and the direct counterpart to the only available mitigation. Any connection to these ports from outside the cluster replication path is an exploitation attempt against a universal compiled-in credential. External-source hits are incidents, not findings.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let clusterPeers = dynamic([]);  // populate with your Expressway cluster node IPs
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (4371, 4372)
| extend PeerKnown = iff(array_length(clusterPeers) > 0 and SourceIP in (clusterPeers), true, false)
| where PeerKnown == false
| extend SourceIsExternal = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Attempts = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 5), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 5)
    by SourceIP, SourceIsExternal
| order by SourceIsExternal desc, Attempts desc

kql.name: Expressway root-level command execution and Erlang service anomalies
kql.description: Exploitation yields root command execution on the Expressway OS. Surfaces shell, interpreter, Erlang and privilege indicators in appliance syslog. Requires Expressway syslog forwarding, which many estates do not have.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("expressway", "expwy", "vcs-", "vcse", "vcsc")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "python", "perl", "root shell", "erlang", "erl_call", "epmd", "cookie", "COMMAND=", "sudo:", "curl", "wget")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Lateral movement from Expressway nodes - SMB, SQL Server and WinRM probing
kql.description: Post-exploitation detection matching the reported chain: custom Python scripts scanning for SMB shares and probing SQL Server and WinRM. Replace expresswayNodes with your actual node addresses before use.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let expresswayNodes = dynamic([]);  // populate with your Expressway node IPs
let targetPorts = dynamic([445, 139, 1433, 1434, 5985, 5986, 3389]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(expresswayNodes) == 0 or SourceIP in (expresswayNodes)
| where DestinationPort in (targetPorts)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), Attempts = count(), PortList = make_set(DestinationPort, 10)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctTargets >= 5 or DistinctPorts >= 3
| order by DistinctTargets desc

kql.name: Bulk access to internal GitLab and source control repositories
kql.description: The reported objective was pulling credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Surfaces access patterns consistent with bulk cloning or scraping rather than developer activity. Adapt the table to your own GitLab logging source.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/gitlab", ".git/", "/api/v4/projects", "/raw/", "/archive", "repository/files", "/-/raw/")
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(csUriStem), Bytes = sum(scBytes), UA = make_set(csUserAgent, 5)
    by cIP, csUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctPaths > 25 or Requests > 200
| order by DistinctPaths desc

kql.name: Windows-side view of inbound enumeration from the video edge segment
kql.description: Catches the same lateral movement from the receiving end, which is valuable where the video edge segment is not covered by firewall logging. Populate videoEdgeSegment with the Expressway node addresses or subnet.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let videoEdgeSegment = dynamic([]);  // populate with Expressway node IPs
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where array_length(videoEdgeSegment) == 0 or RemoteIP in (videoEdgeSegment)
| where LocalPort in (445, 139, 1433, 1434, 5985, 5986)
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 10), Hosts = dcount(DeviceName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by RemoteIP
| order by Hosts desc

kql.name: Credential harvesting and repository cloning tooling on hosts reachable from the video edge
kql.description: Surfaces the generic post-exploitation tooling profile reported in this chain - git cloning, credential scraping utilities and Python one-liners - on Windows hosts that an Expressway node could reach.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git clone", "git config --get", "trufflehog", "gitleaks", "--mirror", "netexec", "crackmapexec", "smbclient", "Invoke-WebRequest", "python -c", "python3 -c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: NEW TO THIS FEED: ConnectWise ScreenConnect CVE-2026-84869 and the SCKit Toolkit - A Month-Long Campaign Against MSP Technician Workstations, 42 Servers and 688,000 Malicious Run-File Requests, and the Patch Is on the Technician Client, Not the Server You Already Updated
affected_products: ConnectWise ScreenConnect technician host client - the vulnerable component
ConnectWise ScreenConnect Access agent
Fixed version: 26.6.5 or later
ScreenConnect server infrastructure is reported NOT affected - updating the server does not remediate the client
ConnectWise has precautionarily disabled five third-party extensions in partner environments
vulnerabilities.summary:
New to this feed and included because it carries the same structural trap as the Outlook zero-day at rank 6, in a channel that reaches UK organisations too small to have a security team of their own: the fix is not where you applied it.

What the flaw is and where it lives. CVE-2026-84869 is a CVSS 9.9 vulnerability in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, disclosed by ConnectWise on 8 September 2026 and added to CISA's KEV catalogue on 11 September. Per ConnectWise's bulletin, it permits unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions. The critical architectural detail is that the vulnerability sits in the TECHNICIAN-SIDE CLIENT, not in the ScreenConnect server. ScreenConnect servers themselves are reported not affected. The consequence is brutal and widely missed: an MSP that dutifully updated its ScreenConnect server infrastructure has not remediated this at all, because the vulnerable software is the host client installed on each of its engineers' workstations. The fix is version 26.6.5 or later, applied to every technician host client and affected Access agent.

The campaign, which is the new material in this window. Huntress has reported a month-long campaign exploiting this flaw against managed service providers. The reported figures are specific: 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers targeted from 29 source IP addresses, with at least 688,000 guest 'run file' requests observed, and activity ongoing since at least 20 October 2026. The attack pattern is that a guest-pushed batch file is executed on a technician workstation; the batch file reaches out to a Telegram bot and installs a rogue ScreenConnect client. Microsoft has separately documented a toolkit it calls SCKit which exploits this CVE to replace the legitimate client with a rogue one. Notably, The Hacker News reports there is no evidence the activity has successfully propagated to a technician workstation or bypassed the vendor patch - which is the single most important caveat in this entry and the reason it ranks fifth rather than first.

Why this matters for UK government and UK corporates, and why it is ranked here. The MSP channel is how cyber risk reaches the parts of the UK public sector that cannot staff a SOC: district councils, GP practices, multi-academy trusts, small NHS suppliers, housing associations. An MSP technician workstation is a credential and access concentrator by design - it holds persistent remote access to every client the engineer supports. A rogue ScreenConnect client installed on that workstation is not one compromise; it is a position from which to reach every customer estate the technician can reach, which is precisely the supply chain shape that produced the worst UK incidents of the last two years. If you are a UK organisation that outsources IT, the question to ask your provider this week is not 'have you patched ScreenConnect', because they will say yes and mean the server. The question is 'are all of your technician host clients on 26.6.5 or later, and can you show me the inventory'.

The mitigation if patching the clients cannot happen immediately. ConnectWise recommends removing TransferFiles permissions across applicable roles and session groups. That is a configuration change on the server that constrains the vulnerable behaviour on the clients, and it is the right stopgap. ConnectWise has also precautionarily disabled five third-party extensions in partner environments.

Why the KEV deadline is in the past. This CVE went into KEV on 11 September with a federal deadline of 2 October 2026. That date has passed, which means for a UK body applying KEV as a standard this is not an upcoming deadline but an overdue one, and the discovery that the server was patched and the clients were not converts a 'closed' ticket into an open finding.

Confidence. High on the CVE, the 9.9 score, the 8 September ConnectWise disclosure, the 11 September KEV addition, 26.6.5 as the fixed version, the technician-client-not-server scope, the TransferFiles permission mitigation, and the existence of the Huntress-reported campaign and the Microsoft-documented SCKit toolkit. Medium on the campaign figures - 42 servers, 29 IPs, 688,000 requests, since 20 October - which trace to Huntress-sourced coverage rather than a primary publication this feed could read. Low on the secondary claim of '400-plus MSP environments breached', which appears only in low-quality aggregators and is not supported by the established outlets. The absence of evidence of successful propagation to a technician workstation is itself reported and is the material caveat.
recommended_actions: Inventory and patch every ScreenConnect TECHNICIAN HOST CLIENT and Access agent to 26.6.5 or later. If you updated your ScreenConnect server and closed the ticket, that ticket should be reopened: the server is not the vulnerable component.

As an immediate stopgap where client patching cannot be completed today, remove TransferFiles permissions across applicable roles and session groups on the server. This constrains the vulnerable behaviour without waiting for every endpoint.

If you are a UK organisation that outsources IT, ask your MSP a specific question in writing this week: are all technician host clients on 26.6.5 or later, and can you provide the inventory. 'We have patched ScreenConnect' is not an answer to this question, because it usually means the server.

Hunt technician workstations for rogue ScreenConnect client installations. Look for ScreenConnect service or client instances that do not correspond to your own instance URL or thumbprint, and for recently installed remote access clients generally.

Hunt for outbound connections to Telegram bot API endpoints from technician workstations and from any host running a remote access client. The reported chain installs the rogue client via a batch file that contacts a Telegram bot, and Telegram API traffic from an engineering workstation is anomalous in almost every UK estate.

Review ScreenConnect session audit logs for guest-initiated 'run file' and file transfer activity, particularly in volume, and especially since 20 October 2026. 688,000 such requests were reported across 42 servers, so even a small share landing in your tenancy would be visible.

Treat this as an overdue KEV item, not an upcoming one. The federal deadline was 2 October 2026. For a UK body applying KEV as a de facto standard, the finding is that this was recorded as remediated when the vulnerable component was never touched.

Check which third-party ScreenConnect extensions you use. ConnectWise has precautionarily disabled five in partner environments, and an extension disabled without warning can break an operational process your service desk depends on.

Rotate credentials stored in or accessible from technician workstations if you find any rogue client, and assume every customer estate that workstation could reach is in scope. An MSP technician endpoint is an access concentrator, so the blast radius is the client list, not the host.

kql.name: Batch file execution originating from ScreenConnect client processes
kql.description: Primary detection for the reported chain: a guest-pushed batch file executed through an active ScreenConnect session. Surfaces cmd.exe and script interpreters whose parent is a ScreenConnect client process.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe", "ScreenConnect.Client.exe", "connectwise")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Telegram bot API traffic from technician workstations and remote access hosts
kql.description: The reported batch file contacts a Telegram bot. Telegram API traffic from an engineering or service desk workstation is anomalous in nearly every UK estate and is the cheapest high-fidelity signal in this entry.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.telegram.org", "telegram.org", "t.me")
| summarize Connections = count(), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Connections desc

kql.name: Installation of ScreenConnect clients not matching your own instance
kql.description: Detects rogue client installation, the reported objective. A ScreenConnect client installed outside your managed deployment path, or carrying an instance identifier you do not recognise, is the finding. Populate knownInstance with your own instance identifier.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let knownInstance = "";  // populate with your ScreenConnect instance identifier or thumbprint
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect", "connectwisecontrol")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| extend SuspectPath = FolderPath has_any ("\\Users\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\AppData\\", "\\ProgramData\\", "\\Downloads\\")
| where SuspectPath or (isnotempty(knownInstance) and not(FileName has knownInstance))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: ScreenConnect client version inventory for patch verification
kql.description: Answers the question this entry exists to raise: are the technician clients, not the server, on 26.6.5 or later. Build the estate inventory from observed process file versions and treat anything below 26.6.5 as unremediated.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe", "ScreenConnect.Client.exe")
| summarize LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Versions = make_set(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, 10), Files = make_set(FileName, 5)
    by DeviceName
| order by DeviceName asc

kql.name: Inbound connections to ScreenConnect servers from the reported source IP population
kql.description: The campaign is reported as 29 source IP addresses against 42 MSP servers. No addresses have been published, so this is a volume and diversity detection rather than a list match: unusual numbers of distinct external sources reaching your ScreenConnect relay ports.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let scPorts = dynamic([8040, 8041, 443, 80]);
let scServers = dynamic([]);  // populate with your ScreenConnect server IPs
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(scServers) == 0 or DestinationIP in (scServers)
| where DestinationPort in (scPorts)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize Sessions = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(SourceIP), Sources = make_set(SourceIP, 50)
    by DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where DistinctSources > 20
| order by DistinctSources desc

kql.name: Credential access and customer-estate reconnaissance from MSP technician workstations
kql.description: Scopes the blast radius question. A technician workstation is an access concentrator; if a rogue client landed there, the next step is customer estates. Surfaces credential tooling and multi-tenant administrative activity from engineering hosts.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let technicianHosts = dynamic([]);  // populate with MSP engineering workstation names
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(technicianHosts) == 0 or DeviceName in~ (technicianHosts)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cmdkey", "vaultcmd", "rundll32 keymgr", "Get-Credential", "mimikatz", "lsass", "Export-PfxCertificate", "net use", "Connect-MsolService", "Connect-AzAccount", "Connect-MgGraph")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
