vulnerabilities.title: TOMORROW: Microsoft Outlook Zero-Day CVE-2026-124194 KEV Deadline Falls on Tuesday 24 November and Its Fix Does NOT Ship Through Windows Update - Plus Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938 and the NHS England Alert Batch Now Including CC-4901 for Ruby
affected_products: Microsoft Outlook (Office desktop clients) - CVE-2026-124194, spoofing, actively exploited zero-day
Fix channel for CVE-2026-124194: the OFFICE updater (Click-to-Run / Microsoft 365 Apps update channels), NOT Windows Update
Java application servers - CVE-2026-114938 'Java4Shell', remote code execution reachable via a Base64 string on Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat servers per secondary reporting
PHP - NHS England Digital cyber alert CC-4900, 19 November 2026, seven critical vulnerabilities; fixed versions include 8.5.13 and 8.4.28
Ruby - NHS England Digital cyber alert CC-4901, 20 November 2026, seven vulnerabilities including three critical in the regular expression engine and string case conversion
Ruby affected versions per CC-4901: 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12, 4.0.0 to 4.0.9; Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not be fixed
vulnerabilities.summary:
Fifth of the five KEV deadlines this feed has been tracking, and the last one to expire: CVE-2026-124194 is due tomorrow, Tuesday 24 November. It is kept at this rank for one reason that has nothing to do with its CVSS score.

The delivery-channel trap, which is the whole point of this entry. CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability, fixed in the November 2026 Patch Tuesday release - the one that addressed 1,235 flaws in total. Its fix ships through the OFFICE update channel, not through Windows Update. The operational consequence is that WSUS, Intune Windows update rings and SCCM compliance reporting will all show your estate as green and compliant while every Outlook client in it remains vulnerable. This is not a theoretical reporting nuance; it is the single most common way UK organisations will miss tomorrow's deadline, and it will happen to organisations with mature patching programmes precisely because they trust their dashboards. Verify Outlook build numbers through the Office update channel - Click-to-Run version reporting, Microsoft 365 Apps admin centre, or the client's own Account page - and treat your Windows Update compliance figure as irrelevant to this CVE.

Why a CVSS 6.5 is ranked above several 9.8s. The flaw leaks NTLMv2 hashes and suppresses the external-content warning that Outlook would normally display. Suppressing the warning is what makes it dangerous: the user-facing control that security awareness training depends on is removed, so there is nothing for a trained user to notice and nothing for them to report. A low-scoring vulnerability that silently harvests authentication material from an estate of tens of thousands of mailboxes is worth more to an attacker than a high-scoring one on an appliance behind a firewall. The compensating control is to block outbound SMB on TCP 445 at the perimeter, which prevents the hash from leaving even where the client is unpatched - and that rule should have existed anyway.

Java4Shell, CVE-2026-114938, held at medium confidence and worth watching rather than panicking about. Reporting in this window describes it as a Java remote code execution flaw where a Base64 string can cause code execution on Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat servers, while a separate roundup states that Java4Shell is proving tricky to exploit in practice. Both of those can be true: a wide theoretical blast radius with a difficult practical path is the profile of a flaw that produces a slow burn rather than a weekend emergency. The sensible posture for a UK estate is to inventory Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat instances this week, because the inventory is the thing you will not be able to build quickly if reliable exploitation does arrive.

The NHS England Digital alert batch, which is the UK-specific delivery mechanism for all of this. CC-4900, dated 19 November, covers seven critical PHP vulnerabilities with fixed versions including 8.5.13 and 8.4.28. CC-4901, dated 20 November and new since this feed's last run, covers seven Ruby vulnerabilities including three critical issues in the regular expression engine and in string case conversion. CC-4901 is rated Medium overall, but note what the NHS England National CSOC says about it: exploitation is assessed as LIKELY and proof-of-concept exploits exist. A Medium-rated alert with likely exploitation and public PoC is exactly the kind of item that gets deprioritised by a severity-driven process. The affected Ruby versions are 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 to 4.0.9; Ruby 3.2 and earlier is end of life and will receive no fix, which is the same end-of-life trap as vCenter 7.0 at rank 1 in a different technology. NHS organisations are required to respond to these alerts within defined timescales, and the PHP and Ruby alerts are the two most likely to land on a web team rather than an infrastructure team - which is where alert response processes tend to break.

The pattern worth naming across ranks 1, 4, 5 and 6. Four of today's six highest-ranked items share a structure: the thing you did does not cover the thing that is vulnerable. vCenter 7.0 has no patch. Expressway needs a firewall rule because the credential cannot be rotated. ScreenConnect's fix is on the client, not the server you updated. Outlook's fix is on the Office channel, not the Windows channel your dashboard reports. If there is one governance action to take out of this report, it is to ask, for each of your top-ten vulnerabilities, where the fix actually lands and whether your reporting can see it.

Confidence. High on CVE-2026-124194's active exploitation, its KEV listing with a 24 November deadline, the Office-updater delivery channel, the NTLMv2 hash leak, the suppression of the external-content warning, the 1,235-flaw November Patch Tuesday total, and the existence and content of NHS England alerts CC-4900 and CC-4901 including the likely-exploitation assessment and PoC existence for CC-4901. Medium on CVE-2026-114938's practical exploitability and on the Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat reachability claim. NHS England Digital pages could not be read directly in this run - all page fetches failed on DNS resolution.
recommended_actions: Verify Outlook build numbers through the OFFICE update channel today, not through Windows Update. Use Click-to-Run version reporting, the Microsoft 365 Apps admin centre or the client Account page. Your WSUS, Intune Windows ring and SCCM compliance figures do not measure this CVE and will mislead you into reporting the estate as remediated.

Block outbound SMB on TCP 445 at the perimeter as the compensating control for CVE-2026-124194. This prevents the NTLMv2 hash from leaving even where a client is unpatched, and it is a rule that should already exist in every UK estate.

Fix the reporting gap permanently rather than just this CVE. Establish a standing Office-channel patch compliance report alongside your Windows one. This is the second time in a month this feed has seen a KEV-deadline item ship outside the channel organisations monitor.

Do not rely on user vigilance for CVE-2026-124194. The flaw suppresses the external-content warning, so there is nothing for a trained user to notice. Awareness messaging about this specific issue is wasted effort; the technical controls are the only controls.

Inventory Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat instances this week for CVE-2026-114938 exposure, including development and build infrastructure that sits outside your production CMDB. Reliable exploitation has not materialised, but the inventory is the part you cannot build quickly later.

Respond to NHS England Digital CC-4900 (PHP) and CC-4901 (Ruby) within the mandated timescales if you are an NHS organisation. Route them to the web and application teams, not just infrastructure - PHP and Ruby alerts commonly fall between the two and are the most frequent cause of missed alert responses.

Treat CC-4901 as higher priority than its Medium rating implies. The NHS England National CSOC assesses exploitation as likely and states that proof-of-concept exploits exist. A severity-driven triage process will under-rank it.

Identify any Ruby 3.2 or earlier in your estate and plan its replacement. It is end of life and will not receive these fixes - the same structural problem as vCenter 7.0 at rank 1, in a different technology and with less visibility.
Review the November Patch Tuesday coverage as a whole. 1,235 flaws in one release means your deployment rings almost certainly have gaps that this month's exception process has not caught up with.

kql.name: Outlook and Office build inventory for the CVE-2026-124194 deadline
kql.description: Answers the question your Windows Update dashboard cannot. Builds an Office client version inventory from the Defender vulnerability management software inventory so you can see which Outlook clients actually carry the fix.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor =~ "microsoft"
| where SoftwareName has_any ("outlook", "office", "microsoft 365 apps")
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 50) by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by SoftwareName asc, SoftwareVersion asc

kql.name: Outbound SMB on TCP 445 leaving the estate - the NTLMv2 leak path
kql.description: Detects the exploitation outcome directly. Any outbound 445 connection to a non-private address is either the compensating control failing or the hash leaving. Treat external destinations as incidents.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemotePort in (445, 139)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| extend IsPrivate = ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP)
| where IsPrivate == false
| summarize Attempts = count(), Destinations = make_set(RemoteIP, 20), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Inbound mail containing UNC paths and SMB-scheme references
kql.description: The delivery side of CVE-2026-124194. Mail referencing external UNC paths or file:// and \\\\host\\share constructions is the lure shape for an NTLM-leaking spoofing flaw.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where Url has_any ("file://", "\\\\", "smb://", "\\\\\\\\")
| join kind=inner (EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(lookback) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound") on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, DeliveryAction, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Base64-bearing requests to Java application server paths - Java4Shell surface
kql.description: Crude but useful first-pass detection for CVE-2026-114938 against Jenkins, Jira and Tomcat front ends. Expect false positives from legitimate encoded parameters; the value is in spotting unusual sources and volumes rather than individual requests.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/jenkins", "/jira", "/manager", "/host-manager", "/rest/api", "/secure/", "/cli", "/script")
| where csUriQuery matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{60,}={0,2}" or csUriStem matches regex @"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{60,}={0,2}"
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 10), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 5)
    by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Requests > 3
| order by Requests desc

kql.name: Child process execution from Java application server processes
kql.description: The reliable detection for any Java deserialisation or expression-injection RCE including Java4Shell. A Java process spawning a shell, interpreter or download utility is the exploitation outcome regardless of the delivery mechanism.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "java", "catalina.sh", "tomcat.exe", "tomcat9.exe", "jenkins.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "sh", "bash", "curl.exe", "curl", "wget", "certutil.exe", "whoami.exe", "whoami")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: PHP and Ruby version inventory against NHS England alerts CC-4900 and CC-4901
kql.description: Supports NHS alert response. Produces the PHP and Ruby version inventory the alerts require, including flagging Ruby 3.2 and earlier as end of life with no fix available.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any ("php", "ruby")
| extend EndOfLifeRuby = SoftwareName has "ruby" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^[0-2]\." or SoftwareVersion startswith "3.0" or SoftwareVersion startswith "3.1" or SoftwareVersion startswith "3.2"
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 50) by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfLifeRuby
| order by EndOfLifeRuby desc, SoftwareName asc, SoftwareVersion asc

vulnerabilities.title: THE UK GOVERNMENT-FACING SOCIAL ENGINEERING WINDOW OPENS TODAY: TfL Asks 60-Plus Oyster Photocard Holders to Return to the Site From 23 November and Will Ask All 265,000 Affected Customers to Reset Passwords and Security Answers, While HMRC Reports 1,704 Self Assessment Scam Reports and a Fake GOV.UK Refund Page
affected_products: Transport for London Oyster photocard online service - portal still offline since 16 November 2026
Approximately 265,000 Oyster photocard accounts assessed as potentially affected
Data potentially compromised per TfL: email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, security questions and answers
Assessed as NOT compromised per TfL: passwords, bank and payment card details, journey histories, and the names and dates of birth of children holding Zip Oyster cards
HMRC Self Assessment service - GOV.UK impersonation; 2025-26 Self Assessment deadline is 31 January 2027
vulnerabilities.summary:
This entry combines two UK government-facing items because they converge on the same thing today, and because the convergence is the finding rather than either item on its own.

The new fact, and it is today. TfL's latest update states that it will ask all photocard customers to change their account password and their security question and answer, and - critically - that it is asking 60-plus photocard holders who are due for an annual address check to revisit the site FROM 23 NOVEMBER. That is today. Read what that creates: a cohort of elderly users, publicly identified by age, publicly told the date they will be asked to return to a website, in the immediate aftermath of a breach in which their email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth and security questions and answers may have been taken. Any attacker reading the same press coverage you are reading now knows the audience, the pretext, the timing and the expected action. The security question and answer exposure is the aggravating factor, because an answer to 'mother's maiden name' or 'first school' cannot be reset in any meaningful sense once known, and the same answers are almost certainly in use at the customer's bank.

The TfL incident status, which has otherwise not advanced. Suspicious activity was detected on 16 November, discovered after customers received emails prompting them to create accounts they already held. TfL assesses around 265,000 photocard accounts as potentially affected. The photocard website remains offline a week on; customers can still travel and top up at machines but cannot reach online accounts. TfL has notified the Information Commissioner's Office, says the incident is contained, and states the investigation continues. It still has not disclosed how the intruders got in. That remains the criticism worth making and it has now stood for a week: without an initial access vector, no other UK public body can check whether it shares the weakness. This is the second major TfL cyber incident in just over two years, following the September 2024 attack.

The HMRC half, which supplies the volume. HMRC published a warning on 17 November reporting 1,704 Self Assessment-related scam reports in the twelve months to 31 October 2026. Roughly 900 of those - about half the total - came from a single August 2026 campaign that used emails carrying a malicious attachment which directed recipients to a counterfeit GOV.UK page built to harvest personal and financial details. HMRC's position is unambiguous and worth repeating verbatim in your own staff and customer communications: it will never contact customers by email, text or phone to tell them they are due a refund, or ask them to claim one. Suspicious emails go to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk, texts to 60599. The 2025-26 Self Assessment deadline is 31 January 2027, which is when HMRC expects this activity to intensify.

Why the two belong in one entry. Both are GOV.UK-brand-adjacent impersonation risks aimed at the general public, both have a known calendar, and both will be delivered through the same channels to the same people. A UK citizen in the next fortnight can expect a plausible TfL email about resetting their photocard security answer and a plausible HMRC email about a tax refund, and the TfL breach has handed attackers the accurate personal detail that makes the first one credible and, by extension, raises the credibility of the second. For UK public bodies the lesson is operational rather than technical: when you tell the public to expect a communication on a specific date, you have published a phishing window. The mitigation is to say, in the same breath and in every channel, exactly what the real communication will and will not contain and ask, and to ensure that what you actually send matches it - no shortened links, no third-party survey domains, no unexpected sender addresses.

Confidence. High on the TfL figures and data categories, the 16 November detection, the portal still being offline, ICO notification, the password and security answer reset instruction, the 60-plus annual address check from 23 November, the absence of any disclosed initial access vector, and the 2024 precedent. High on the HMRC 1,704 figure, the roughly 900 attributable to the August campaign, the malicious attachment and fake GOV.UK page mechanism, HMRC's never-contacts-you position, and the reporting channels. Medium on whether the 265,000 figure will hold - it is TfL's own 'may have been compromised' estimate rather than a confirmed count. No evidence yet exists of a phishing campaign specifically exploiting the TfL breach, which is why this entry's exploitation status is attempts reported but unconfirmed; the prediction is this feed's, not a reported fact.
recommended_actions: If you are a UK public body with a scheduled public communication, publish exactly what it will and will not contain at the same time as you publish the date. TfL has told the public when to return to its site; that is a published phishing window, and the only mitigation is making the real message distinguishable in advance.

Audit your own outbound communications against the advice you give. No shortened links, no third-party survey or marketing domains, no unexpected sender addresses, and a sender domain the public can verify. Organisations routinely tell customers to distrust the exact patterns their own marketing teams use.

If your organisation uses security questions and answers for identity verification anywhere, stop treating them as a secret for anyone affected by this breach. The TfL exposure includes security questions and answers, those answers are reused at banks and utilities, and a reset does not make a known answer unknown.

Brief your own service desk and customer contact teams that callers may now hold accurate personal detail - home address, date of birth, phone number - for a large population. Knowledge-based verification is weaker this week than it was last week.

Repeat HMRC's position verbatim in staff and public communications ahead of the 31 January 2027 Self Assessment deadline: HMRC will never contact customers by email, text or phone to say they are due a refund, or ask them to claim one. Report suspicious emails to phishing@hmrc.gov.uk and texts to 60599.

Hunt inbound mail referencing TfL, Oyster, photocard, HMRC refunds and GOV.UK in your own tenancy, including to staff personal-adjacent addresses where you have visibility. Public-sector staff are in the affected population too, and a credential harvested from a personal lure gets reused.

Add lookalike domain monitoring for TfL, Oyster and GOV.UK-adjacent strings if you operate any related service. The August HMRC campaign used a counterfeit GOV.UK page, which means the registration pattern is already proven to work against this audience.

Keep asking TfL, through whatever channel you have, for the initial access vector. A week without it means no other UK public body can determine whether it shares the weakness, and that is a sector-wide cost of one organisation's disclosure choice.

Record in your risk register that security question and answer compromise is unremediable by reset, and use this incident as the evidence to retire knowledge-based verification where you still rely on it.

kql.name: Inbound mail impersonating TfL, Oyster photocard or GOV.UK services
kql.description: Primary detection for the predicted campaign. Looks for the brand vocabulary of both halves of this entry in inbound mail, with sender domain surfaced so lookalikes stand out against the genuine domains.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
let genuineDomains = dynamic(["tfl.gov.uk", "hmrc.gov.uk", "gov.uk", "service.gov.uk"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any ("oyster", "photocard", "transport for london", "tfl", "security question", "self assessment", "tax refund", "hmrc", "gov.uk")
| extend SenderLooksGenuine = SenderMailFromDomain in~ (genuineDomains)
| where SenderLooksGenuine == false
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, ThreatTypes, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Lookalike domains in mail referencing UK government and transport brands
kql.description: Catches the counterfeit GOV.UK page pattern that HMRC reported in its August campaign. Surfaces URLs whose host resembles but does not match the genuine domains.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
let genuineHosts = dynamic(["tfl.gov.uk", "oyster.tfl.gov.uk", "hmrc.gov.uk", "www.gov.uk", "gov.uk"]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| extend Host = tostring(parse_url(Url).Host)
| where Host has_any ("tfl", "oyster", "photocard", "hmrc", "gov-uk", "govuk", "gov.uk")
| where Host !in~ (genuineHosts)
| summarize Messages = dcount(NetworkMessageId), Urls = make_set(Url, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by Host
| order by Messages desc

kql.name: Endpoint connections to lookalike UK government and transport domains
kql.description: Catches the click that mail filtering missed. A connection from a managed device to a host that resembles a UK government or TfL domain without matching one is a credential-entry candidate.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
let genuineHosts = dynamic(["tfl.gov.uk", "oyster.tfl.gov.uk", "hmrc.gov.uk", "www.gov.uk", "gov.uk", "service.gov.uk"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("tfl", "oyster", "photocard", "hmrc", "govuk", "gov-uk")
| extend Host = tostring(parse_url(strcat("https://", RemoteUrl)).Host)
| where RemoteUrl !has_any (genuineHosts)
| summarize Connections = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName), Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 20) by RemoteUrl
| order by Connections desc

kql.name: Credential stuffing and password spray against accounts matching the affected population
kql.description: The TfL exposure includes email addresses, dates of birth and security answers. Where staff personal details overlap with your directory, reuse-driven credential stuffing is the follow-on risk. Surfaces failure patterns consistent with it.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType in ("50126", "50053", "50055", "50056", "50076")
| summarize Failures = count(), DistinctUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 30), Countries = make_set(Location, 10)
    by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctUsers >= 5 or Failures >= 25
| order by DistinctUsers desc

kql.name: Self-service password and security information resets at anomalous volume
kql.description: If a lure succeeds, the attacker's next step is often to change the recovery path. This surfaces self-service reset and authentication-method change activity at volumes or times that do not fit normal patterns.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where OperationName has_any ("Self-service password reset", "Reset password", "User registered security info", "User changed default security info", "Admin registered security info", "User deleted security info")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| summarize Events = count(), Operations = make_set(OperationName, 10) by Actor, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where Events > 2
| order by Events desc

vulnerabilities.title: NEW: Rackspace Spot Breach - Leaked Credentials Gave Attackers Legitimate-User Access to Customer Kubernetes Clusters for Nearly 22 Hours, Every Secret and API Token in Affected Clusters Must Be Treated as Compromised, and the Admin Console Outage Stopped Customers Rotating Them
affected_products: Rackspace Spot - cloud Kubernetes platform
Customer Kubernetes clusters hosted on Rackspace Spot
Spot API tokens and refresh tokens used in automation tooling
Kubernetes Secrets stored in affected clusters
Kubernetes configuration files (kubeconfig) issued for affected clusters
vulnerabilities.summary:
The one new item in this window that comes with hard, machine-ingestible indicators - which, after three consecutive runs in which this feed could publish nothing but behavioural and provenance notes, is worth saying first.

What happened. Rackspace has told customers that an unauthorised party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot, its cloud Kubernetes platform, on 17 November 2026. The intrusion window is given as approximately 00:20 to 22:00 UTC that day - roughly twenty-two hours. Rackspace learned of it on 18 November after a customer report, not through its own detection.

What the attacker could do, which is the part that matters. In some customer organisations the intruders operated as legitimate users. They could create pods in Kubernetes clusters, READ KUBERNETES SECRETS, and list nodes and volumes. Rackspace's own guidance is the clearest statement of impact available: any Secret in affected clusters, together with Spot API tokens and refresh tokens, should be treated as compromised. That is a platform-level compromise of the secret store, which in practice means database passwords, cloud provider keys, registry credentials, TLS private keys and service account tokens - whatever your teams put in Kubernetes Secrets, which in most organisations is everything.

The detail that turns this from an incident into a lesson. The breach also caused an extended outage of the Spot administration console, which temporarily prevented customers from managing clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials. Service was announced as fully restored on 21 November. Sit with that sequence: the credentials were exposed, the customer was told to rotate them, and the mechanism for rotating them was unavailable because of the same incident. Every UK organisation running workloads on a managed Kubernetes platform should take one question away from this - if our provider's control plane were down, could we rotate our secrets by another route? For most the answer is no, and the fix is to hold a break-glass path that does not depend on the provider's console: direct API access with an independently stored token, infrastructure-as-code that can re-provision secrets, or a secret manager outside the cluster.

Rackspace's response. It revoked tokens, rotated keys and removed unauthorised pods, and instructed customers to reissue Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tooling, download fresh kubeconfig files, and rotate credentials stored in cluster Secrets. It also advised reviewing logs for databases, container registries, Git repositories and cloud storage back to 17 November - which is the right instruction, because the value of a stolen Secret is realised somewhere else.

The indicators. Rackspace has published an attacker IP address, 23.224.79.106, and an associated range, 23.224.0.0/15, together with suspicious Kubernetes pod and object name prefixes: i1, glm- and probe. These are the first hard network and object indicators this feed has been able to publish in four runs. They are reported consistently across multiple secondary accounts of Rackspace's customer notification; this feed could not read the notification itself because all direct page fetches failed on DNS resolution, so verify before deploying as a blocking rule. The /15 range in particular should be reviewed before blocking, as a /15 is a large allocation and may contain unrelated services.

UK relevance, stated honestly. Rackspace has a substantial UK presence and a long history as a hosting provider to UK businesses and public sector bodies, and Spot is a low-cost spot-instance Kubernetes offering of exactly the kind that development teams adopt without a procurement conversation. No UK organisation has been named, Rackspace has not disclosed how many customers were affected, and it has not said whether data was exfiltrated or whether the credentials belonged to a customer, an internal account or a platform service identity. So the UK exposure here is unquantified. It is included at this rank because the action required is cheap, specific and time-bounded, and because shadow Kubernetes is a real feature of UK public sector development estates.

Confidence. High on the incident, the 17 November window of approximately 00:20 to 22:00 UTC, discovery on 18 November via customer report, the legitimate-user access level, the ability to create pods and read Secrets and list nodes and volumes, Rackspace's treat-as-compromised guidance, the specific remediation instructions, the console outage preventing rotation, and restoration on 21 November. Medium on the indicators, which come from consistent secondary reporting of the customer notification rather than from the notification itself. Unknown: customer count, exfiltration, the origin of the leaked credentials, and whether any UK organisation is affected.
recommended_actions: If you run anything on Rackspace Spot, rotate every Kubernetes Secret in affected clusters today. Rackspace's own guidance is to treat all of them as compromised, which includes database passwords, cloud provider keys, registry credentials, TLS private keys and service account tokens.

Reissue Spot API tokens and replace every refresh token embedded in automation tooling, CI/CD pipelines and infrastructure-as-code. Refresh tokens in automation are the ones organisations forget, and they are the ones that provide durable access.
Download fresh kubeconfig files for all affected clusters and invalidate the old ones. A kubeconfig issued before 17 November should be assumed to be in someone else's hands.

Block or alert on 23.224.79.106 and review the 23.224.0.0/15 range before blocking it wholesale. Verify against Rackspace's own notification first: a /15 is a large allocation and may contain unrelated services, so an unreviewed block carries availability risk.

Hunt for Kubernetes pods and objects whose names begin with i1, glm- or probe across all clusters, not only those you believe were affected. These are the published attacker object prefixes and are cheap to search for.

Review logs for databases, container registries, Git repositories and cloud storage back to 17 November 2026, as Rackspace advises. A stolen Secret is used somewhere other than where it was stolen, so the cluster logs are not where you will find the consequence.

Establish a break-glass secret rotation path that does not depend on your provider's console. The console outage in this incident prevented customers from rotating the very credentials they had just been told were compromised. Direct API access with an independently stored token, or a secret manager outside the cluster, both solve it.

Move secrets out of Kubernetes Secrets and into an external secret manager with short-lived dynamic credentials where you can. Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default, and this incident shows what platform-level read access to them costs.

Find your shadow Kubernetes. Spot is a low-cost spot-instance platform of the kind development teams adopt without procurement involvement. Ask your development leads directly rather than consulting the CMDB, which will not know.

Note in your supplier assurance records that discovery came from a customer report rather than provider detection, and that the provider has not disclosed the customer count or whether data was exfiltrated. Those are legitimate questions to put to the provider in writing.

kql.name: Traffic to or from the published Rackspace Spot attacker infrastructure
kql.description: Direct indicator match on the published address and range. Verify the range against Rackspace's own notification before converting this into a blocking rule, since a /15 is a large allocation.
kql.query:
let attackerIp = "23.224.79.106";
let attackerRange = "23.224.0.0/15";
let lookback = 60d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SourceIP == attackerIp or DestinationIP == attackerIp
    or ipv4_is_in_range(SourceIP, attackerRange) or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, attackerRange)
| extend ExactMatch = (SourceIP == attackerIp or DestinationIP == attackerIp)
| summarize Events = count(), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 20), Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, DestinationIP, ExactMatch
| order by ExactMatch desc, Events desc

kql.name: Endpoint-side connections to the attacker range
kql.description: Catches the same infrastructure from managed endpoints and build agents, which is where a CI/CD runner using a stolen Spot token would appear.
kql.query:
let attackerRange = "23.224.0.0/15";
let lookback = 60d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| where ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, attackerRange)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Kubernetes audit and container runtime events referencing the attacker object prefixes
kql.description: Searches for the published pod and object name prefixes i1, glm- and probe. Run this against all clusters, not only those believed affected - it is cheap and the cost of missing a rogue pod is high.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let prefixes = dynamic(["i1", "glm-", "probe"]);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("kube-apiserver", "kubelet", "containerd", "CreatePod", "pods", "secrets")
| where SyslogMessage has_any (prefixes)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Pod creation and Secret read activity across the intrusion window
kql.description: Scoped to 17 November 2026. The reported capability was creating pods and reading Secrets as a legitimate user, so the hunt is for activity that looks authorised but has no owner. Adapt the table to your Kubernetes monitoring source.

kql.name: Downstream use of credentials that were stored in Kubernetes Secrets
kql.description: The most important query in this entry. A stolen Secret is used somewhere other than the cluster, so this looks for service and automation identities authenticating from new networks after 17 November.
kql.query:
let incidentDate = datetime(2026-11-17);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > incidentDate - 30d
| where isnotempty(AccountDisplayName)
| where AccountDisplayName has_any ("svc-", "service", "automation", "ci", "pipeline", "runner", "k8s", "kube", "spot")
| extend Period = iff(Timestamp < incidentDate, "before", "after")
| summarize IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), Events = count() by AccountDisplayName, Period
| order by AccountDisplayName asc, Period asc

kql.name: Cloud control-plane activity from unfamiliar sources after the incident date
kql.description: If cloud provider keys were held in affected Kubernetes Secrets, the consequence appears in the cloud control plane rather than in the cluster. Surfaces post-17-November activity from caller IP addresses not previously seen for each identity.
kql.query:
let incidentDate = datetime(2026-11-17);
let baseline = AzureActivity
    | where TimeGenerated between (incidentDate - 90d .. incidentDate)
    | summarize KnownIPs = make_set(CallerIpAddress, 200) by Caller;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated >= incidentDate
| join kind=leftouter baseline on Caller
| where CallerIpAddress !in (KnownIPs)
| summarize Operations = count(), Ops = make_set(OperationNameValue, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
    by Caller, CallerIpAddress
| order by Operations desc

vulnerabilities.title: UK CORPORATE AND SUPPLIER CLUSTER: N0n Posted Two More UK Victims TODAY Including a Licence-Plate-Recognition Analytics Firm, Halfords Data Is Now Listed as Exposed, and the Belfast Supplier Wellington IT Has Put Roughly 40 Credit Unions Into Breach Notification
affected_products: Claimed by N0n and listed 23 November 2026: 'Company #250' - described as a UK licence-plate recognition analytics firm, marked pending exposure
Claimed by N0n and listed 23 November 2026: 'Company #254' - described as a UK online fashion and homewares retailer, marked pending exposure
Claimed by N0n, listed 20 November 2026: Halfords Group plc - described as the semantic search index of a major UK retailer, now marked NOT PAID / EXPOSED, attack estimated 9 November
Claimed by N0n, listed 17 November 2026: Bensons for Beds (bensonsforbeds.co.uk); Debenhams listed with attack estimated 9 November
Claimed by Qilin, listed 21 November 2026: ION Asset Architecture UK Ltd, attack estimated 9-16 November (tracker dates inconsistent)
Claimed by Qilin, listed 9 November 2026: amberman.co.uk
Claimed by TheGentlemen, listed 3 November 2026: bsfgroup.co.uk
Claimed, listed 20 November 2026: William Cook Holdings Limited (William Cook Group), UK defence manufacturer, attack estimated 4 November
Confirmed by the supplier, not a leak-site claim: Wellington IT, Belfast - CU Online platform, approximately 40 Irish credit unions plus a small number in Northern Ireland
vulnerabilities.summary:
Carried at deliberately LOW confidence, because almost everything in it is attacker self-reporting and because this feed has documented that the group responsible inflates its numbers. Read the caveats before you read the names.

The new listings, which are dated today. Ransomware.live records N0n posting two further UK victims on 23 November 2026, both anonymised and both marked pending exposure: 'Company #250', described as a licence-plate recognition analytics firm, and 'Company #254', described as an online fashion and homewares retailer. The first of those is the one worth a second look. UK licence-plate recognition analytics is a small sector that sits unusually close to government: automatic number plate recognition data is processed for police forces, local authority enforcement, car parks, clean air and congestion zones, and private estate management. An ANPR analytics provider holds vehicle movement data, which is location data about identifiable individuals at scale. If this claim is genuine - and no organisation has been named, let alone confirmed - the dataset class is materially more sensitive than the retail listings around it. It is also a supplier category that most UK public bodies would struggle to find in their own supplier registers, because ANPR analytics is typically procured as part of an enforcement or parking contract rather than as an IT service.

The Halfords listing has changed state. Halfords Group plc, listed by N0n on 20 November with an attack estimated at 9 November, is now marked NOT PAID / EXPOSED on the tracker, having previously been pending. The listing describes the data as the semantic search index of a major UK retailer. That description continues the asset class this feed flagged on 22 November and it remains the genuinely novel element of this cluster: vector indexes, semantic search corpora, AI storefront assistant conversation logs and storefront service identities. Almost no UK organisation has these in an asset inventory, almost none has them in a data protection impact assessment, and a semantic search index built over a retailer's catalogue and customer interactions is a derived dataset that may contain more than its owner realises. Halfords has not confirmed an incident.

The credibility problem, restated because it is the most important thing in this entry. Bitdefender's analysis of N0n's own exposed file server indicated just over twenty real victims against more than one hundred listings, and 126 entries removed from October's totals. Victim counts for N0n across trackers range from roughly 189 to 259 depending on collection method, which is itself evidence that nobody has a reliable figure. SOCRadar characterises N0n as a financially motivated extortion group that emerged in September 2026, focused on data theft rather than encryption, and using credentials harvested by third-party infostealer malware for initial access. That last point is the actionable part of the whole entry: if the group's access route is infostealer-harvested credentials, then the defence is not patching but credential hygiene - phishing-resistant MFA, session token lifetime, and monitoring for your own domains in infostealer log dumps.

The item in this cluster that is NOT a claim. Wellington IT, a Belfast-based provider that processes member account data on behalf of credit unions, has confirmed a cybersecurity incident affecting information stored in its CU Online platform. Reporting puts the intrusion at 2 to 4 October 2026, with an attacker using an automated script to send millions of malicious requests. The exposed data appears limited to payee details - the names, account numbers and addresses of people and businesses that members pay, rather than the account holders' own data. Around 40 breach notifications from credit unions have reportedly reached Ireland's Data Protection Commission; a small number of Northern Ireland credit unions also use the platform. Minister Robert Troy publicly criticised the notification delay, saying it was a major concern that the company only made the credit unions aware the previous day. This is a UK-headquartered supplier whose single platform compromise created roughly forty downstream regulatory notifications across two jurisdictions, roughly six weeks after the intrusion. That is the supply chain concentration risk the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill at rank 3 is partly aimed at, demonstrated in the same week MPs vote on it.

Other UK listings in the window, recorded for completeness and not individually verified: ION Asset Architecture UK Ltd (Qilin, listed 21 November, tracker dates internally inconsistent), William Cook Holdings Limited (UK defence manufacturer, listed 20 November, attack estimated 4 November), Debenhams and Bensons for Beds (N0n), amberman.co.uk (Qilin, 9 November) and bsfgroup.co.uk (TheGentlemen, 3 November).

Confidence. LOW overall and by design. High only on: the existence and dates of the leak-site listings, Bitdefender's documented inflation of N0n's victim count, SOCRadar's characterisation of the group's access route, and the Wellington IT incident including the supplier's own confirmation, the CU Online platform, the payee-data scope, the roughly forty notifications and the ministerial criticism. Medium on the October 2 to 4 intrusion dates and the millions-of-requests method, which are single-source. Low on every leak-site victim claim, every description of the stolen data, and every attack-date estimate. No UK organisation named in the leak-site portion of this entry has confirmed an incident, and this feed has not been able to reach any primary source directly in this run.
recommended_actions: Treat every leak-site claim in this entry as unverified. Bitdefender documented N0n inflating its victim count by roughly a factor of five, and tracker totals for the group vary by seventy victims depending on collection method. Do not brief a board on a claim without saying this.

Act on the group's reported ACCESS ROUTE rather than its victim list. SOCRadar assesses N0n as using credentials harvested by third-party infostealer malware. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, shorten session token lifetimes, and subscribe to monitoring for your own domains appearing in infostealer log dumps. That is the defence; patching is not.

Add vector indexes, semantic search corpora, AI assistant conversation logs and storefront service identities to your asset inventory and your data protection impact assessments. The Halfords listing describes a semantic search index, and almost no UK organisation currently records these as assets even though they are derived datasets that may contain more than their owner realises.

If you are a UK public body, find out whether your enforcement, parking or clean-air contracts involve an ANPR analytics provider, and who it is. The 23 November listing claims a UK licence-plate recognition analytics firm. ANPR analytics is usually procured inside an enforcement contract rather than as an IT service, so it is typically absent from supplier security registers.

Ask any ANPR or vehicle-movement analytics supplier directly whether they are affected, and what their retention period is for movement data. Vehicle movement data is location data about identifiable individuals at scale, which makes the dataset class materially more sensitive than the retail claims alongside it.

If your organisation uses Wellington IT's CU Online platform, confirm whether you are in the affected population and whether you have a notification obligation. A small number of Northern Ireland credit unions use the platform, so this is a UK regulatory question as well as an Irish one.

Use the Wellington IT case in your own supplier assurance work. One platform compromise produced roughly forty downstream regulatory notifications across two jurisdictions, notified roughly six weeks after the intrusion. Ask your own critical suppliers what their notification timescale commitment is, in writing, and what happens if they miss it.

Do not pay attention to the ordering of leak-site listings as a measure of severity. The listings in this cluster are ordered by the attacker's publication schedule, which is an extortion tactic, not an assessment of impact.

Monitor for the two anonymised listings being de-anonymised. N0n marks listings as pending exposure before publishing; if 'Company #250' is named and is a supplier to a UK police force or local authority, the assessment in this entry changes materially.

kql.name: Sign-ins consistent with infostealer-harvested credentials - the reported N0n access route
kql.description: The most directly useful query in this entry. Infostealer-derived access typically shows a valid credential from an unfamiliar network, often with a cloned user agent and without MFA interaction. Tuned for successful sign-ins rather than failures.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
let baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(30d))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize KnownAsns = make_set(AutonomousSystemNumber, 100), KnownCountries = make_set(Location, 50) by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=leftouter baseline on UserPrincipalName
| where AutonomousSystemNumber !in (KnownAsns) or Location !in (KnownCountries)
| extend MfaSatisfied = AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| where MfaSatisfied == false
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, Location, AutonomousSystemNumber, IPAddress, UserAgent, AppDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Infostealer execution and browser credential store access
kql.description: Addresses the upstream cause rather than the symptom. Surfaces access to browser credential and cookie stores, which is how infostealers collect the credentials this group reportedly buys.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName has_any ("Login Data", "Cookies", "Web Data", "logins.json", "key4.db", "cert9.db", "Local State")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe", "MsMpEng.exe", "SenseIR.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Bulk export from semantic search, vector index and AI assistant services
kql.description: Covers the novel asset class in this cluster. Vector indexes and AI assistant conversation corpora are rarely monitored because they are rarely inventoried. Adapt the service names to your own stack.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where Application has_any ("search", "vector", "elastic", "opensearch", "pinecone", "weaviate", "qdrant", "algolia", "azure cognitive search", "ai search")
    or ObjectName has_any ("index", "embedding", "vector", "corpus", "conversation")
| where ActionType has_any ("Export", "Download", "Scroll", "Bulk", "FileDownloaded", "SearchQueryPerformed")
| summarize Actions = count(), Objects = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 10)
    by AccountDisplayName, Application, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Actions > 200 or Objects > 50
| order by Actions desc

kql.description: Matches the reported Wellington IT method - an automated script sending millions of malicious requests over roughly two days. Detects the shape rather than a signature, so it generalises to any portal-facing scripted abuse.

let lookback = 90d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(csUriStem), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 5), Bytes = sum(scBytes)
    by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 2000
| order by Requests desc

kql.name: Outbound data volume anomalies to file sharing and transfer services
kql.description: N0n is characterised as a data theft and extortion group that does not rely on encryption, so exfiltration volume is the detection rather than ransomware behaviour. Compares each source against its own recent baseline.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
let baseline = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(14d))
    | summarize AvgDaily = avg(SentBytes) by SourceIP;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)

vulnerabilities.summary:
The board entry: everything with a deadline, everything with an evidence problem, and the items that matter but did not earn a rank of their own.

THE DEADLINE BOARD. Expiring TODAY, Monday 23 November: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 (rank 1), Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (rank 4), Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884. Expiring TOMORROW, Tuesday 24 November: Microsoft Outlook CVE-2026-124194 (rank 6). Already PASSED and therefore overdue rather than upcoming: SonicWall SonicOS CVE-2026-19868 (20 November) and ConnectWise ScreenConnect CVE-2026-84869 (2 October, rank 5). Still ahead: Perforce Puppet Enterprise CVE-2026-115731 (1-2 December) and Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 (9 December). No new KEV additions were recorded between 21 and 23 November; the last batch was the four added on 20 November.

GL.iNET - NEW, EXPLOITED, AND THE NOTICE WAS UPDATED TODAY. GL.iNet has confirmed that attackers exploited a flaw in its cloud remote management service, reported as GoodCloud, to install malware on routers and KVM devices. Its security notice is dated 20 November 2026 and was UPDATED on 23 November. Users have found backdoors and reverse shells giving root-level control. GL.iNet says it has patched the cloud service and blocked the attack path, and here is the critical sentence: PATCHING THE CLOUD SERVICE DOES NOT REMOVE MALWARE ALREADY ON DEVICES. Stable security firmware is available and reportedly removes the identified malware without a factory reset, with thresholds reported as 4.11.1 or later for several router lines and 1.10.3 or later for most KVM devices. Three caveats make this worse than it first reads. First, GL.iNet has not said how the attackers got in, how many devices were affected, or whether data was stolen, and is still investigating whether computers attached to infected KVMs were compromised - a KVM sits between an administrator and a server console, so a compromised KVM is a keystroke and screen capture position on whatever it fronts. Second, one consultancy reports that GL.iNet's own detection checks may miss some infections and that it could not detect the malware using GL.iNet's published indicator. Third, researchers separately found an unrelated older backdoor on 49 managed routers installed between September 2025 and May 2026 by an unknown route, with one consultancy reporting 166 of 199 analysed routers affected by one issue or the other. GL.iNet devices are common in UK small offices, home-worker setups, test labs and temporary sites - the places that sit outside the asset register.

APACHE ROLLER CVE-2026-129448 - the fake mitigation, repeated because it keeps catching people. Disabling XML-RPC through the Roller admin interface DOES NOT MITIGATE this flaw, because affected versions deserialise the request before checking the feature flag. The real mitigation is setting enabledForExtensions=false in WEB-INF/web.xml or removing the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, then restarting. The affected range is 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 - an eighteen-year span, not the single 6.1.5 release that earlier reporting suggested - and the correct patch target is 6.1.7, released 11 November 2026 with fifteen further CVE fixes, not 6.1.6. Public proof-of-concept code predates the Apache advisory by about seven weeks, so an instance that has been internet-facing since late September should be hunted, not merely patched. Its KEV deadline is today.

SAP NETWEAVER CVE-2025-42884 - the evidence-quality problem. KEV-listed on 20 November with a deadline today, on a patch that is roughly a year old. No IOCs, no attribution and no proof-of-concept have been published by SAP, CISA or Onapsis, and at least one source states that no public evidence of exploitation exists. This feed records it as exploited on the strength of the KEV listing alone and says so plainly. If you run NetWeaver Enterprise Portal, patch it today because the deadline is real; but if you are asked to evidence the threat to a change board, the honest answer is that the only evidence is CISA's determination.

APACHE TOMCAT CVE-2026-133325 - new, critical, and nobody agrees on the score. Published 19 November 2026, this is a key exchange without entity authentication flaw (CWE-322) allowing an unauthenticated node to join a Tomcat cluster secured with TLS 1.3 and TLS-PSK. Apache rates it Critical. One source cites CVSS 9.8; others state no CVSS score is published or call it unscored. It is NOT in KEV and no public exploit has been reported. Affected versions are listed as 11.0.28-11.0.29, 10.1.62 and 9.0.124, with fixes in 11.0.30, 10.1.63 and 9.0.125; Apache's interim recommendation is switching cluster encryption to TLS 1.2 with TLS-PSK. The scope caveat is important and reduces the practical urgency considerably: this only matters if you run Tomcat clustering with TLS-PSK over TLS 1.3, and a default installation has neither a cluster nor a TLS-PSK channel. Rated here as informational-to-watch rather than urgent, with the scoring disagreement recorded rather than resolved.

SONICWALL CVE-2026-19868 - overdue, and the UK exposure is in the gap between 'we have MFA' and 'MFA is enforced'. An authentication enforcement flaw in SonicOS SSLVPN: an attacker holding valid credentials for an alternative authentication method can bypass SAML authentication controls INCLUDING SAML-ENFORCED MFA. It only affects SSLVPN where SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins. CISA added it to KEV on 6 November with a deadline of 20 November, which has passed; HKCERT reports active exploitation, while SonicWall says only that its PSIRT investigated a report of potential exploitation - the third vendor-versus-authority split in today's report. Gen7 is affected through 7.3.3-7015 and fixed in 7.3.4-7013; Gen8 is affected through 8.2.2-8015 and fixed in 8.2.3-8015. No workarounds exist. Sources disagree on severity, one giving CVSS 7.1 and SonicWall's advisory reportedly 8.8; check SNWLID-2026-0014. SonicWall firewalls are widespread in UK SMEs, schools, GP practices and smaller councils, and an MFA bypass in a remote access product is the single most consequential control failure in that segment.

CARRIED, QUIET, AND STILL WORTH FIVE MINUTES: NGINX2Root. Still no KEV listing and still no confirmed exploitation. Rapid7's own PoC README warns it will likely fail against servers with multiple concurrent clients, which is what a production nginx estate is - that is the explanation for the quiet. Blacklisting the unused SCTP kernel module remains the highest-value five-minute action available anywhere in this report, because the escalation stage has no CVE, no upstream patch and no scanner coverage, which means no vulnerability management tool will ever tell you about it. While you are there, audit Alpine and musl container base images for OpenSSH below 10.6p2 - SSHole lets an oversized password bypass authentication entirely, and most organisations assess SSH exposure against servers rather than base images.

ALSO IN THE WINDOW, NOT RANKED. Google Chrome CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free in the XML component and the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, fixed in 157.0.8103.50/.51. Cleverbridge has confirmed theft of payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV/CVC codes, notifying customers from 20 November, with no disclosed cause or victim count. Bell Canada has confirmed enterprise customer data theft from a 17 November intrusion involving what it describes as an agentic threat actor. The FBI's National Crime Information Center has reportedly been breached, the second reported FBI systems breach in two months. Signal has shipped protections blocking screenshots on iOS 27 and preventing AI assistants capturing conversations on supported Android. A Scottish hacker has been sentenced to six years in a US prison. Cribl Stream CVE-2026-115873 is listed at CVSS 9.9 and TOTOLINK A7100RU CVE-2026-134882 at CVSS 10 on the 23 November CVE Brief, neither with a UK angle established. Considered and not ranked for lack of a UK link or any November development: the New Zealand Defence Force website intrusion, the 3AM ransomware attack on a UK school estate (September attack, disclosed 3 November, no new information), UK Government Investments' 51-official data exposure, the Gibraltar government cloud intrusion, and the Gleneagles Hotel listing, for which no corroborating reporting could be found.

CLOSED OR ROTATED OUT THIS RUN: the RDM refrigeration operation (no new substance; NCSC advice unchanged - patch, change default credentials, get the devices off the internet), the UK offensive cyber disclosure via General Sir Rob Magowan (no development since 20 November), N-able (no new information), and OPTIMJACK/Optimizely, which closed on 22 November with all monitored files clean since 16 November. The HSBC lesson from that incident is retained as the week's most transferable finding: its content security policy blocked the main malicious script while a backup copy still ran.

Confidence. MEDIUM overall, deliberately, because this entry aggregates items of very different evidence quality and the point of it is to show that. High on all KEV dates and deadlines, the Roller mitigation failure and version range, the GL.iNet confirmation and firmware thresholds, the Tomcat version and fix list, and the SonicWall affected and fixed firmware versions. Medium on the GL.iNet detection-unreliability claim and the 166-of-199 router figure, and on the Tomcat CVSS score. Low on SAP NetWeaver exploitation, which rests solely on the KEV listing.
recommended_actions: Close out today's four expiring deadlines before close of business: vCenter CVE-2026-123890, Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466, Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884. Tomorrow adds Outlook CVE-2026-124194. Anything not done needs a written risk acceptance with a named owner, not a rollover.

If you run GL.iNet routers or KVM devices, update firmware now - 4.11.1 or later for routers and 1.10.3 or later for most KVMs - and understand that GL.iNet patching its cloud service did NOT remove malware already on your devices. The firmware is reported to remove the identified malware without a factory reset.

Treat any GL.iNet KVM as a keystroke and screen-capture position on whatever server console it fronts. GL.iNet is still investigating whether attached computers were compromised, so assume credentials typed through an affected KVM are exposed and rotate them.

Do not rely on GL.iNet's own detection check alone. One consultancy reports it may miss infections and that it could not detect the malware using GL.iNet's published indicator. Where a device cannot be verified clean, reflash or replace it.

If you run Apache Roller, verify the mitigation you applied actually works. Disabling XML-RPC through the admin UI does NOT mitigate CVE-2026-129448. Set enabledForExtensions=false in WEB-INF/web.xml or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, restart, and patch to 6.1.7 - not 6.1.6. If you checked only for version 6.1.5 you checked the wrong thing: the range is 4.0.0 onward.
Hunt rather than just patch any Roller instance that has been internet-facing since late September 2026. Public PoC code predates the Apache advisory by about seven weeks.

Patch SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal for CVE-2025-42884 today because the deadline is real, but tell your change board the truth about the evidence: no IOCs, no attribution and no PoC have been published by SAP, CISA or Onapsis, and the only basis for the exploitation claim is CISA's determination.

Check whether you actually run Tomcat clustering with TLS-PSK over TLS 1.3 before treating CVE-2026-133325 as urgent. A default Tomcat installation has neither a cluster nor a TLS-PSK channel. If you do, upgrade to 11.0.30, 10.1.63 or 9.0.125, or switch cluster encryption to TLS 1.2 with TLS-PSK as Apache recommends.

Check SonicWall SSLVPN firmware against CVE-2026-19868 today - its deadline passed on 20 November. Gen7 needs 7.3.4-7013 or later, Gen8 needs 8.2.3-8015 or later, there are no workarounds, and the flaw bypasses SAML-ENFORCED MFA. Then review SSLVPN authentication logs for logins via alternative authentication methods.

Blacklist the unused SCTP kernel module. Five minutes, no service restart negotiation, and it removes the privilege escalation stage of the NGINX2Root chain - a kernel flaw with no CVE, no upstream patch and no scanner coverage, which is why no vulnerability management tool will ever surface it.

Audit Alpine and musl container base images for OpenSSH below 10.6p2. SSHole lets an oversized password bypass authentication entirely, and most organisations assess SSH exposure against servers rather than base images.

Confirm Chrome is on 157.0.8103.50 or later across the estate. CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, and browser patch compliance is the control most often assumed rather than measured.

kql.name: Apache Roller XML-RPC endpoint access - exploitation and fake-mitigation verification
kql.description: Serves two purposes: detects exploitation attempts against /roller-services/xmlrpc, and verifies whether your mitigation actually works. If you disabled XML-RPC in the admin UI and requests are still being processed with a 200 response, your mitigation has failed.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/roller-services/xmlrpc", "xmlrpc", "/roller-services")
| summarize Requests = count(), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), Methods = make_set(csMethod, 5), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by cIP, csUriStem
| order by Requests desc

kql.name: Java child process execution on Roller, Axis and Tomcat hosts
kql.description: Covers Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448, Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 and any Tomcat deserialisation path with one query. A Java process spawning a shell or download utility is the exploitation outcome regardless of the delivery vector.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe", "javaw.exe", "java", "catalina.sh", "tomcat.exe", "tomcat9.exe", "tomcat10.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "sh", "bash", "curl.exe", "curl", "wget", "certutil.exe", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: GL.iNet device outbound activity to non-vendor cloud and command-and-control candidates
kql.description: GL.iNet has published no attacker infrastructure, so this detects the shape instead: a small office router or KVM initiating outbound connections to destinations other than the vendor's own cloud. Populate glinetDevices with your device addresses.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
let glinetDevices = dynamic([]);  // populate with GL.iNet router and KVM IPs
let vendorDomains = dynamic(["gl-inet.com", "goodcloud.xyz", "glddns.com"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(glinetDevices) == 0 or SourceIP in (glinetDevices)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| where isempty(DestinationHostName) or DestinationHostName !has_any (vendorDomains)
| summarize Sessions = count(), Destinations = make_set(DestinationIP, 30), Hosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 20), BytesOut = sum(SentBytes)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by Sessions desc

kql.name: Reverse shell and persistent outbound sessions from network appliance segments
kql.description: GL.iNet users reported backdoors and reverse shells giving root-level control. This surfaces long-lived outbound sessions from appliance segments, which is the network signature of a reverse shell regardless of the device type.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
let applianceSegments = dynamic([]);  // populate with router, KVM and appliance management subnets
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(applianceSegments) == 0 or SourceIP in (applianceSegments)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| summarize Sessions = count(), Duration = max(TimeGenerated) - min(TimeGenerated), BytesIn = sum(ReceivedBytes), BytesOut = sum(SentBytes)
    by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort
| where Duration > 1h and Sessions < 20
| order by Duration desc

kql.name: SonicWall SSLVPN logins via alternative authentication methods - CVE-2026-19868 bypass
kql.description: Detects the exploitation outcome for the SonicWall MFA bypass. The flaw lets a credential for an alternative authentication method bypass SAML-enforced MFA, so the signal is SSLVPN authentication succeeding through a non-SAML path where SAML is configured.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("sonicwall", "snwl", "firewall", "sonicos")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("SSLVPN", "SSL VPN", "ssl-vpn")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("login", "authenticated", "logged in", "user login")
| extend SamlPath = SyslogMessage has_any ("SAML", "saml")
| summarize Logins = count(), Samples = make_set(SyslogMessage, 5) by Computer, SamlPath, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| order by TimeGenerated desc, SamlPath asc

kql.name: Consolidated KEV deadline exposure across this report's CVE set
kql.description: The management view. Produces per-CVE device counts for every KEV item in this report so the deadline board can be reported as a number rather than a narrative. Extend the list as new items are added.
kql.query:
let kevCves = dynamic(["CVE-2026-123890", "CVE-2026-76466", "CVE-2026-129448", "CVE-2025-42884", "CVE-2026-124194", "CVE-2026-19868", "CVE-2026-84869", "CVE-2026-115731", "CVE-2026-90436", "CVE-2026-125350", "CVE-2026-133325"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in (kevCves)
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 50), Software = make_set(SoftwareName, 10), Severity = any(VulnerabilitySeverityLevel)
    by CveId
| order by Devices desc

kql.name: Alpine and musl base image OpenSSH version audit for SSHole
kql.description: Supports the five-minute container action. SSHole lets an oversized password bypass authentication entirely, and most organisations assess SSH exposure against servers rather than base images, which is where it hides.
kql.query:
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any ("openssh", "ssh")
| extend VersionMajor = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend VersionMinor = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend BelowThreshold = VersionMajor < 10 or (VersionMajor == 10 and VersionMinor < 6)
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 50) by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, BelowThreshold
| order by BelowThreshold desc, Devices desc

Four genuinely new items (Entra Connect Health, ScreenConnect/SCKit, Rackspace Spot, GL.iNet) and the first hard network indicators in four runs. summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Six things. The first four have federal remediation deadlines that expire TODAY and the fifth expires tomorrow. (1) PATCH VCENTER TODAY, THEN HUNT ANYWAY. CVE-2026-123890's KEV deadline is today. Fixed builds are 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m, and this is not eligible for Quick Patch. Re-read VMSA-2026-0009.1 rather than the 19 November original, because Broadcom revised it on 20 November to clarify affected VMware Tools versions. If you are on 7.0 there is no public patch and never will be: 7.0 left general support in October 2025, so today is a three-option decision with a named owner - buy extended support and raise a Broadcom case, accelerate migration to 8.0 U3m or VCF 9.1, or isolate. Block TCP 2012 at the firewall either way, because Broadcom has confirmed no configuration change mitigates this and that rule is the only control that exists. Then hunt, because ARMORY CASTLE held access from early September to the 19 November fix: enumerate every vsphere.local SSO administrator against change records, check for access to /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb, and decide this week whether to rotate SAML STS signing material, because an attacker holding it can mint valid assertions and no password reset revokes that. (2) BLOCK TCP 4371-4372, THEN AUDIT YOUR GITLAB. Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 also expires today, and Cisco disclosed it on 21 October - the fix has been available five weeks. The Erlang cookie is compiled in and identical on every install, so reachability is the entire exposure and blocking needs no maintenance window. Upgrade clustered nodes to X15.5.20, treat every cluster peer as compromised if any node was reachable, and then act on the chain: attackers harvested credentials from internal GitLab repositories, so patch the appliance and skip the repositories and you have closed the door and left the keys outside. (3) CHECK OUTLOOK THROUGH THE OFFICE UPDATER, NOT WINDOWS UPDATE. CVE-2026-124194's deadline is tomorrow and its fix ships through Office's own channel, so WSUS, Intune Windows rings and SCCM compliance will all report your estate green while every Outlook client stays vulnerable. It is only CVSS 6.5, it leaks NTLMv2 hashes, and it suppresses the external-content warning, which means user training has nothing to act on. Block outbound SMB on 445 as the compensating control and fix the reporting gap permanently. (4) REOPEN THE SCREENCONNECT AND ROLLER TICKETS YOU CLOSED. ScreenConnect CVE-2026-84869's vulnerable component is the TECHNICIAN CLIENT, not the server your MSP updated, and its KEV deadline passed on 2 October - ask your provider in writing whether every technician host client is on 26.6.5 or later and demand the inventory. For Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448, disabling XML-RPC in the admin UI does NOT mitigate it: set enabledForExtensions=false in WEB-INF/web.xml or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc mapping and restart, patch to 6.1.7 rather than 6.1.6, and note the affected range is 4.0.0 onward rather than 6.1.5 alone. (5) TELL YOUR GLOBAL ADMINISTRATORS, BY A CHANNEL THAT IS NOT EMAIL. Attackers read tenant ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope and licence tier together with your global administrator and technical contact addresses out of Microsoft's Entra Connect Health API between 23 July and 19 November. There is no patch because the vulnerable component was Microsoft's. What there is, is a verified target list: the next lure will name your organisation, your onmicrosoft.com domain and your administrator correctly, and will be accurate in every detail they would normally check. Harden the help-desk verification path for privileged resets this week, and hunt consent grants and privileged-role changes across the exposure window. (6) ROTATE EVERY KUBERNETES SECRET ON RACKSPACE SPOT, AND BLOCK 23.224.79.106. Attackers operated as legitimate users in customer clusters for around twenty-two hours on 17 November and could read Secrets; Rackspace says treat every Secret, API token and refresh token as compromised.
